look_for.title: Dakar's CICES trade fair
look_for.text: Look for the triangle motif its French architects repeated at every level, from the site plan down to the cross-section of the handrails.

look_for.title: Jean Léon's spaceship auditorium
look_for.text: His concrete auditorium for Lycée Mamie Adjoua, a girls' school in Yamoussoukro, looks ready for take-off, shown beside drawings from his sketchbooks.

look_for.title: Senghor's unbuilt Musée des Civilisations Noires
look_for.text: Drawings and an original model for the museum Senegal's president never got to build sit in a small gallery between the fairs and the universities.

look_for.title: James Barnor's trade-fair photographs
look_for.text: His pictures of the Africa Pavilion at the 1967 Ghana International Trade Fair in Accra hang in the event-architecture room.

exhibitions.title: Tone
exhibitions.description: A group show of nineteen artists, including Roy DeCarava, Kerry James Marshall and Lorna Simpson, exploring tone, from black to white and every value between, as an expressive material language.
exhibitions.long_description:
Everything here comes from the Studio Museum's own collection: about twenty works in black, white and the values between, from an undated daguerreotype to an embossed paper piece Chiffon Thomas made this year. Not all of it is photography. You also get Larry Walker in charcoal, a Chris Ofili silkscreen, a Yiadom-Boakye oil and a Paul Anthony Smith drawn in graphite on stoneware. Zanele Muholi's self-portrait was made on 116th Street, nine blocks south, if you want to see it in colour afterwards.

No critic has reviewed it yet. Admission is pay-what-you-can ($16 suggested), free on Sundays and for under-16s, and the museum stays open until 9pm on Fridays.

look_for.title: Kerry James Marshall, Naomi
look_for.text: Look at the highlights: Marshall swapped the photograph's whites for tints of purple and soaked the shadows in blue-black.

look_for.title: Glenn Ligon, Stranger #86
look_for.text: Coal dust mixed into oil stick and gesso builds a field of very dark black, from a series named after Baldwin's "Stranger in the Village".

look_for.title: An unidentified daguerreotype
look_for.text: A seated Black woman with a steady gaze, her dark dress and pale scarf on a silver plate that tarnish has turned warm sepia.

look_for.title: Gary Simmons, Lean / To
look_for.text: A wooden shack drawn in black lines of different weights, then smudged and erased with cartoon speed lines so it seems to be disappearing.

look_for.title: Lorna Simpson, Appeared
look_for.text: Figures from 1950s to 1970s Ebony and Jet hair ads surface and recede through washes of three different blues, alongside her recurring iceberg.

exhibitions.title: A Sustained Becoming: Studio Museum Artists in Residence 2026
exhibitions.description: The first Artist-in-Residence cohort in the Studio Museum's new building: Derriann Pharr, Simonette Quamina and Taylor Simmons use figuration across mediums to explore cultural memory and time.
exhibitions.long_description:
All three start from the figure, then go separate ways. Pharr builds fluid, ambiguous mixed-media figures that resist naturalistic likeness. Quamina makes monumental prints and collaged graphite drawings out of a childhood spent between the Caribbean, South America and New York. Simmons layers acrylic, oil, airbrush and wax, sampling music, photographs and viral content into scenes of masculinity and youthful play. That is a better use of viral content than the screenshots folder you will never open.

No critic has reviewed it yet. The museum describes real and otherworldly images that evoke remembering or dreaming. It runs to 3 January 2027, with late hours until 9pm on Fridays. Admission is pay-what-you-can, $16 suggested for adults.
exhibitions.editors_pick: A year of studio work by the 2026 artists in residence, Derriann Pharr, Simonette Quamina and Taylor Simmons, among the first shows in the Studio Museum's new Adjaye building: figurative work on cultural memory and time.

exhibitions.title: Arthur Jafa: I Am Tony
exhibitions.description: Jafa's inaugural US museum survey spans nearly four decades of work, including "Love is the Message, The Message is Death" and the Golden Lion-winning "The White Album," alongside new pieces exploring Black life in America.
exhibitions.venue_address: 235 Bowery, New York, NY 10002, United States
exhibitions.long_description:
Curators Massimiliano Gioni and Gary Carrion-Murayari spread nearly four decades across two floors, mostly in near-darkness. Love Is the Message, The Message Is Death, his best-known video, sits in a small side gallery where its song is barely audible over the other videos' screams and rumbles. Carrion-Murayari told Arts Fuse the show is "not only images of Black death and trauma; there's also images of Black creativity."

Admission is $25, with pay-what-you-wish hours on Thursday evenings. Two videos run long, AGHDRA at 1 hour 14 minutes and akingdoncomethas at 1 hour 45, so you won't see everything in one visit.
exhibitions.editors_pick: Arthur Jafa's first US museum survey, close to four decades of work, including Love Is the Message, the Message Is Death, his seven-minute montage of Black American life cut to Kanye West's Ultralight Beam.

look_for.title: Monster
look_for.text: A 1988 self-portrait of Jafa pointing his camera at a mirror and looking up, so his reflection and the viewer's gaze meet.

look_for.title: MBD\_Trans Am
look_for.text: A Pontiac Trans Am, part of it crushed and left beside the intact front half, with a booming sound that ARTnews calls both alluring and repellent.

look_for.title: Notebooks
look_for.text: A hallway of binders holding images cut from books and magazines; one pairs an MF DOOM album ad with a Cindy Sherman photograph of her in a silvery mask.

look_for.title: The Last Wave
look_for.text: A wall-filling mural where the Alien Xenomorph sits beside a solar eclipse, a New Order album cover, Michael Jackson performing and Billie Holiday in her coffin.

look_for.title: AGHDRA and the Picture Unit
look_for.text: In a large dim gallery, a computer-generated ocean full of broken rocks stutters and reverses, next to a walk-in maze whose walls are lined with images, including white eyes peering from a void.

exhibitions.title: There Are No Words: Si Lewen's Parade
exhibitions.description: Conceived by Si Lewen (1918–2016) in the aftermath of World War II, The Parade is informed by the artist's extraordinary life.
exhibitions.long_description:
The Parade is 63 charcoal, pencil and ink drawings Si Lewen made around 1950, a wordless novel after Frans Masereel's woodcuts. There are no captions: "just the picture itself is the narrative," Lewen said. You read it by walking around the gallery, and curator Maria Castro describes sparse scenes of small groups giving way to dense, dark, chaotic ones. Lewen, a Jewish refugee from Germany, went back as one of the Ritchie Boys and reached Buchenwald just after its liberation in 1945.

Reviewing the cycle at James Cohan Gallery in 2024, David D'Arcy saw "the absurd pomp and horror of war" told with the punch of comics. The Met bought it that year, and this is its first showing here: one room, Gallery 690, free with Museum admission, through 5 January.

look_for.title: The parade horse
look_for.text: Look for the army horse in full dress regalia at the head of the march, leaving its droppings as part of the pageant.

look_for.title: The children who watch
look_for.text: Early drawings show children gazing at the soldiers in awe; a few frames later they are led away.

look_for.title: The scratched battle frames
look_for.text: War arrives as abstract lines scratched into the surface, then explosions, then destruction and boxes of bodies carried off.

exhibitions.title: Guggenheim Pop: 1960 to Now
exhibitions.description: A sweeping survey of Pop art from the 1960s to today, with works by Warhol, Lichtenstein, Oldenburg, Hamilton and Chryssa shown alongside a Yayoi Kusama Infinity Mirror Room and recent contemporary acquisitions.
exhibitions.venue_address: 1071 Fifth Avenue, New York, NY 10128, United States
exhibitions.long_description:
The show takes four tower galleries on three floors. Tower 5 holds the 1960s, under Oldenburg and van Bruggen's 26-foot shuttlecock feathers. Tower 7 is built around Kusama, and level 4 has the recent acquisitions, Cattelan's taped banana included. You pass Marta Minujín's drawings for a Statue of Liberty laid on her side in Battery Park and covered in McDonald's patties, next to the letter turning it down.

ArtNowLA called the historical works "the show's strongest cards", and Highbrow's Sandra Bertrand found it "worth a concentrated look". It's included in museum admission. For the Kusama room, scan a QR code on arrival to join the virtual queue: groups of up to four get 60 seconds, entry isn't guaranteed, and the queue closes once full, so come early.

look_for.title: Soft Shuttlecock
look_for.text: Nine canvas-and-foam feathers, each 26 feet long, sprawl across the Tower 5 gallery, made for Oldenburg's 1995 rotunda retrospective and unseen in New York for 25 years.

look_for.title: The Kusama mirror room
look_for.text: On Tower Level 7, mirrors multiply flickering lights in every direction, and for part of your 60 seconds the lights go out completely.

look_for.title: Cattelan's Comedian
look_for.text: A single banana duct-taped to the wall in the contemporary galleries on level 4, a promised gift to the museum.

look_for.title: Jim Dine's Bedspring
look_for.text: A bedspring Dine found near Washington Square Park in 1960, built up with newsprint, burlap and lightbulbs.

look_for.title: Warhol's Orange Disaster #5
look_for.text: A grid of the same newspaper photograph of an electric chair, silkscreened over and over in orange.

exhibitions.title: The Lost World: The Art of Minnie Evans
exhibitions.description: A touring retrospective of self-taught artist Minnie Evans's work from 1935-1981: vibrant drawings, paintings and collages blending spiritual imagery with natural motifs, made in North Carolina during the Jim Crow era.
exhibitions.long_description:
You start with her first two pen drawings, from 1935, titled My Very First and My Second, and the show runs in order to the dense, mandala-like pictures she made from the 1960s on, more than 100 works in all. During wartime rationing she drew on found Coast Guard stationery and a window shade. She titled one 1963 drawing Modern Art, and in 1975 the Whitney put it on the cover of her exhibition brochure.

Labels are in English and Spanish, with Bloomberg Connects audio and verbal descriptions for several works. Admission is $30, free for visitors 25 and under, on Friday evenings from 5 to 10pm and on second Sundays.

look_for.title: Invasion Picture (1944)
look_for.text: A mound of skulls and a Mosquito combat aircraft over a watery landscape like Wilmington's coast, painted after a vision in which she heard God tell her to "draw or die".

look_for.title: Airlie Oak (1954)
look_for.text: The Airlie Gardens oak, a tree dating to at least 1545, built up in layers of dried paint she scraped from old cans and thinned with turpentine, on a wooden crate lid.

look_for.title: The turnaround pictures
look_for.text: Crayon drawings symmetrical on both axes, made to hang and be viewed from any orientation, with feathered forms, pincher forms and eye pendants.

look_for.title: Modern Art (1963)
look_for.text: White angels stand guard over an altar-like centre of long pine trees, winged beasts, mandalas and cryptic writing, framed by decorative curves.

look_for.title: Minnie Evans Art 1981
look_for.text: A 57-page scrapbook, one of her last works, with her self-portrait on the cover and, inside, drawings, photographs, letters and the 1969 Newsweek article that called her a "beautiful dreamer".

exhibitions.title: Collection in Focus: Modern European Currents
exhibitions.description: Early 20th-century European avant-garde painting drawn from the collection, with works by Kandinsky, Goncharova, Franz Marc and others who reimagined painting for a rapidly changing world.
exhibitions.venue_address: 1071 Fifth Avenue, New York, NY 10128, United States
exhibitions.long_description:
This is one gallery of the museum's own collection, mostly painted between 1910 and 1918 by artists from the German, Austro-Hungarian and Russian empires. You can follow Kandinsky from four landscapes of the Bavarian village of Murnau to Painting with White Border (1913), where his native Moscow is still recognisable but most of the canvas has gone abstract. Goncharova, Popova, Malevich and Schiele cover the more radical turns. The watercolors rotate because they are too fragile to stay out, so what's on paper depends on when you go.

In the Wall Street Journal, Judith H. Dobrzynski called it "enlightening". It's small, nearly twenty paintings and watercolors by the museum's count, and included in general admission ($30, under-12s free, pay what you wish Tuesdays and Sundays 4 to 5:30pm).

look_for.title: Franz Marc's Yellow Cow
look_for.text: A yellow cow with a full udder, painted to Marc's idea that yellow is "the female principle, gentle, gay, and sensual", as the wall label explains.

look_for.title: Kandinsky's Painting with White Border
look_for.text: Look for signs of Moscow, which Kandinsky had just revisited in 1913, half-dissolved into the abstract colour that fills most of the canvas.

look_for.title: Kandinsky's Murnau landscapes
look_for.text: Four views of the Bavarian village, in colours as intense as Gabriele Münter's but with freer, less blocky shapes.

look_for.title: Marc's White Bull
look_for.text: A white bull from 1911, painted when Marc and the Blue Rider artists wanted art to express the spirituality of nature and animals.

look_for.title: Campendonk's Farmer with Horse and Wagon
look_for.text: A farmer with his horse and wagon, painted in 1918 and never shown since it entered the collection in 1948.

exhibitions.title: Costume Art
exhibitions.description: Inaugurating the new Conde Nast Galleries, the Costume Institute pairs nearly 400 garments with paintings and sculpture to explore how art has depicted the dressed body.
exhibitions.long_description:
The Costume Institute's new galleries, nearly 12,000 square feet off the Great Hall where the gift shop used to be, sort about 400 objects into body types: naked, classical, pregnant, aging, disabled, mortal. Garments stand beside art from across the Met, so Van Gogh's Irises hangs between a Yves Saint Laurent and a Loewe ensemble. This is the Met Gala's show, and the Gala's dress code was "Fashion is Art". Here you can wear sneakers.

Critics split. Wallpaper called it "a compelling and deeply researched exhibition"; ARTnews found most pairings "vague and sloppy" and gave it "a failing grade". Come for the clothes and the pairings that click. It's in Gallery 099, included with Met admission ($30, pay what you wish for New York State residents), and open until 9pm Fridays and Saturdays.

look_for.title: McQueen's wooden legs for Aimee Mullins
look_for.text: Look for the carved timber prosthetic boots Alexander McQueen made in 1999 for the Paralympian, in the section on the disabled body.

look_for.title: Gaultier's SAFE SEX FOR EVER shirt
look_for.text: A 1997 Gaultier shirt and a 1971 Joe Brainard drawing both show heart tattoos splayed across a man's chest; ARTnews called this pairing the show's most powerful.

look_for.title: Nicole Kidman's Moulin Rouge! dress
look_for.text: The black Gaultier she wore to the 2001 premiere stands beside Adam McEwen's fake obituary painting of Kidman, in which she wears the same dress.

look_for.title: The Gucci uterus dress
look_for.text: Alessandro Michele's Gucci dress, with a uterus appliqué, is paired with a small Egyptian carnelian figurine in the pregnant body section.

look_for.title: Irises between two ensembles
look_for.text: Van Gogh's Irises hangs flanked by a 1988 Yves Saint Laurent haute couture look and a Loewe look from spring 2025.

exhibitions.title: David Lamelas: The Machine
exhibitions.description: A comprehensive survey of Argentine Conceptual artist David Lamelas, tracing his work from 1965 to today across film, sculpture and performance, unfolding as exhibition, film program and live work.
exhibitions.long_description:
You then walk into a darkened east gallery: a clock set to Moon time, a projector beam where the work is the space between lamp and floor, and silent films measuring a gallery against its city. The west gallery centres on his 1968 Venice Biennale news office about the Vietnam War. A separate film program includes the view from a taxi on the FDR Drive, timed to the second, with nobody asking for a tip.

Artforum called the show "masterfully orchestrated", and Revista Exclama described the looking it asks for as slow and analytical, so give it time. Entry is free, Wednesday to Saturday, 12 to 6pm, with public tours at 1pm on 14 November, 12 December and 9 January.

look_for.title: Untitled (Falling Wall)
look_for.text: Look for the large drywall panel propped on larch-wood supports at the entrance, leaning as if caught mid-collapse.

look_for.title: Moon Time
look_for.text: In the darkened east gallery, a standard clock tells you the time on the Moon instead of in Manhattan.

look_for.title: Límite de una proyección II
look_for.text: A projector throws a beam of light onto the floor, and Lamelas says the work is the space between the two, not the light.

look_for.title: Office of Information About the Vietnam War
look_for.text: His 1968 Venice news office of desk, telex and microphone, restaged without its glass screen and visible from the West 22nd Street window.

look_for.title: To Pour Milk into a Glass
look_for.text: A 1972 video in which milk is poured into a glass until it overflows.

exhibitions.title: Zeng Fanzhi
exhibitions.description: Zeng Fanzhi's first New York exhibition in over a decade: a new sculpture and a suite of new paintings of imagined celestial landscapes, at the 22nd Street gallery.
exhibitions.long_description:
The one sculpture is an obelisk of blue onyx, banded blue and cream, and the gallery says it looks like something dug out of one of the planets in the paintings around it. Those paintings are imagined landscapes from another world, in Zeng Fanzhi's first New York show in over a decade.

Each canvas gives you two pictures. From across the room, colour laid side by side rather than mixed on the palette pulls together into rock formations, water and pitch-black horizons. Walk up close and it breaks apart into fields of pure pigment. Zeng paints wet-on-wet with several brushes at once, so every new layer drags through the one still drying underneath, and the press release compares the result to both pointillism and the pixelation of digital images.

It follows his show in Venice during the 2024 Biennale. Entry is free with no booking at 542 West 22nd Street, Tuesday to Saturday, 10am to 6pm, from the opening reception on Thursday 5 November, 6 to 8pm.

look_for.title: The blue onyx sculpture
look_for.text: Look for an obelisk-like standing form in blue and cream banded quartz, made to read as an artifact excavated from the planets in the paintings.

look_for.title: The black horizons
look_for.text: Beyond jagged rock and water, pitch-black skies open out, with streaks of turquoise, yellow and deep crimson glinting like fossils or bioluminescent fragments.

look_for.title: The grids
look_for.text: Precise grids and lines run across several canvases like survey maps or excavation plans, then get churned up by the brushwork laid over them.

exhibitions.title: Elmgreen & Dragset: TRANSITION
exhibitions.description: Elmgreen & Dragset debut a 40-ton, traversable steel sculpture with a new series of wall works, on the performative side of architecture. At Pace's 508 and 510 West 25th Street spaces.
exhibitions.long_description:
-   [Li Hei Di: the year of mud6 November 2026 – 19 December 2026](https://www.musa.guide/en/discover/new-york/exhibitions/pace-gallery/li-hei-di-the-year-of-mud)
-   [David Byrne: Stairwell Drawings10 April 2025 – 31 December 2026](https://www.musa.guide/en/discover/new-york/exhibitions/pace-gallery/david-byrne-stairwell-drawings)
-   [Lucas Samaras: Boxes and Reconstructions6 November 2026 – 23 January 2027](https://www.musa.guide/en/discover/new-york/exhibitions/pace-gallery/lucas-samaras-boxes-and-reconstructions)

exhibitions.title: Coumba Samba: Stars and Stripes
exhibitions.description: The inaugural solo museum presentation of Senegalese American artist Coumba Samba, an immersive installation examining nuclear power and African resource extraction through symbols of the U.S. military-industrial complex.
exhibitions.long_description:
It is one installation, made for this room by the Harlem-born Samba (born 2000), and her first solo museum show. The label lists acrylic on extruded polystyrene, oil on wood, an electric fan and an LED light. You get the history from the wall text: the Congo's Shinkolobwe mine supplied most of the uranium for the Hiroshima bomb, and in 2003 a claim that Iraq had sought 500 tons of ore from Niger helped justify the invasion.

Samba calls the piece "bright and dark". The Floor 1 gallery is free to everyone during Museum hours, so you can walk in without a ticket. The Whitney is closed Tuesdays.

look_for.title: The uranium-shell sculptures
look_for.text: Monumental freestanding forms modeled on depleted uranium shells fill the centre of the gallery, each striped in the colours of one of five national flags.

look_for.title: The Congo's colours
look_for.text: Look for the blue, red and yellow of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which the wall text ties to the Shinkolobwe mine and the uranium for the Hiroshima bomb.

exhibitions.title: Siena: The Art of Bronze, 1450-1500
exhibitions.description: Nearly forty Renaissance bronzes, including works by Donatello and Francesco di Giorgio Martini, exploring the innovations of Sienese sculptors in the second half of the 15th century.
exhibitions.long_description:
Nearly forty bronzes fill the three Lauder Exhibition Galleries: statues, reliefs, candelabra and medals, many never shown outside Tuscany. The first room covers foundry practice and bell casting, the second Donatello's stay in Siena from 1457 to 1461, and the largest the funerary sculpture, portrait medals and statues. Several works sit in open-backed cases that show the casting behind them.

Galerie called it "by no means blockbuster-sized, but rather a well-curated jewel box", and the New Criterion calls it the first survey anywhere of Siena's bronze masters. Admission is $30 and the Frick recommends timed tickets. It runs until 18 January.
exhibitions.editors_pick: Donatello's bronze tomb slab for Bishop Pecci, from Siena Cathedral, on its first trip to the United States. Around it, nearly 40 bronzes cast in Siena between 1450 and 1500. Best for anyone who already loves the Frick's own bronzes.

look_for.title: Donatello's tomb slab for Bishop Pecci
look_for.text: A bronze funerary slab of Giovanni di Bartolomeo Pecci, one of only eight signed Donatello works, shown in the US for the first time.

look_for.title: The Mariano Sozzini the Elder monument
look_for.text: The only surviving bronze effigy of a layman from 15th-century Italy, a tomb figure of a lawyer rather than a bishop.

look_for.title: Vecchietta's Resurrection, 1472
look_for.text: Christ rising from the tomb in a bronze relief the dealer Joseph Duveen gave Henry Clay Frick, a major source of inspiration for the show.

look_for.title: Hercules Triumphing over the Nemean Lion
look_for.text: A late-1480s statuette about 16 inches tall, attributed to Francesco di Giorgio, one of three Hercules bronzes with newly clarified dating.

look_for.title: Francesco di Giorgio's Lamentation
look_for.text: A bronze about 86 by 75 cm, c. 1475, of the Lamentation at the foot of the cross, lent from Santa Maria del Carmine in Venice.

exhibitions.title: The Surrealist Book: Tomorrow Lives in Mirrors
exhibitions.description: A survey of Surrealism's book-as-art-object experiments by André Breton, Salvador Dalí, Claude Cahun, Max Ernst and others, built around a major gift of rare artists' books from the Helen and Sam Zell Collection.
exhibitions.long_description:
The galleries are on MoMA's third floor, their walls written over with lines of poetry facing cases full of books. The show is anchored by the Zell Collection, about 100 artists' books given to MoMA in 2022 and shown here for the first time. You walk it in date order: Breton, Dalí and Éluard making books together in the 1920s and 30s, Toyen printing in secret in Nazi-occupied Prague, then Burroughs and Gysin after the war. Some books stand on pedestals like sculpture.

Expect glass between you and the pages: the most fragile volumes can only be leafed through on interactive screens. The catalogue is $75 at the MoMA store.

look_for.title: Hugnet's mercury binding
look_for.text: Look for L'Air de l'eau, whose cover holds liquid mercury between glass plates painted as a seabed with fish, so the picture changes whenever the book moves.

look_for.title: The book-objects on pedestals
look_for.text: Look for bindings treated as sculpture: one book holds sand and works as an hourglass when turned over, others have mirrors, seahorses or fossils set into their covers.

look_for.title: Toyen's wartime books from Prague
look_for.text: Made in secret under Nazi occupation with homemade photographic techniques; of one volume only six or seven copies survive, and four of them are here.

look_for.title: Man Ray and Éluard's Facile (1935)
look_for.text: Man Ray's solarized nudes run into the lines of Éluard's love poems on the same page.

look_for.title: Miró's A Toute Épreuve (1958)
look_for.text: Miró's colourful, blob-like woodcuts float around Éluard's poems across the spreads.

exhibitions.title: Lucas Samaras: Boxes and Reconstructions
exhibitions.description: Lucas Samaras's box sculptures of the 1960s to 1980s alongside never-before-seen fabric paintings from his 1979 Reconstructions series.
exhibitions.long_description:
As a boy in Greece, Samaras would sit in his cousin's dress shop cutting up paper, and whenever he reached for the fabric she told him not to touch it. In 1979, with nobody to stop him, he sewed fabric into big, busy paintings he called Reconstructions. They stayed in his own collection, and this is the first time any have been shown. You still can't touch the fabric.

They hang beside his boxes, a series of almost 300 he kept making from the early 1960s into the 1980s. He fixed photographs, cutlery, nails, mirrors, bright yarn and feathers onto boxes full of compartments and drawers, using liquid aluminum and plaster. The selection runs from the plain hinged Box #5 to Stiff Box #14, all curves in Cor-ten steel, and Box #133 from 1989.

Nobody has reviewed it yet. Entry is free at Pace's Chelsea building, 540 West 25th Street, Tuesday to Saturday, 10am to 6pm, with an opening reception on 5 November from 6 to 8pm.

look_for.title: The Reconstructions (1979)
look_for.text: Hand-sewn fabric paintings crowded with clashing patterns, colours, textures and shapes, from the artist's own collection and never shown before.

look_for.title: Box #5 (1963–1968)
look_for.text: The plainest box in the room: a rectangular construction that opens on hinges, from the early years of the series.

look_for.title: Stiff Box #14 (1971)
look_for.text: A box in Cor-ten steel, its sides bent into curves Pace calls sinuous yet sinister.

exhibitions.title: Hyundai Translocal Series: Ho Tzu Nyen
exhibitions.description: A new site-specific video work by Singapore-based artist Ho Tzu Nyen installed in the museum's OMA-designed elevators, part of an ongoing series exploring power, endurance, and transformation.
exhibitions.venue_address: 235 Bowery, New York, NY 10002, United States
exhibitions.long_description:
That is the whole exhibition: P for Power: Up Down, a new commission by Ho Tzu Nyen, playing on screens inside the museum's glass-front elevators, which look out onto the Bowery. A sister piece with 24 projectors opens at the Ulsan Art Museum in Korea on October 22. It's the only elevator in Manhattan where pressing the button again actually changes something.

Time Out called it "a fitting introduction to a lineup that gets considerably weirder from there," and that's the right way to take it: part of the ride up to Jafa, Marcon and the Bowery show. It comes with general admission, free for 18 and under, pay what you wish Thursdays 7 to 9pm.

look_for.title: The child on the elevator screen
look_for.text: Look for a life-size, digitally rendered Singaporean child who appears when you press a button and delivers a mantra, question, riddle or note about power.

look_for.title: A new sequence every press
look_for.text: Each time someone presses a floor button, an AI system generates a fresh image sequence in real time, so riding twice gets you something different.

exhibitions.title: Screens Series: Umi Ishihara
exhibitions.description: The US institutional debut of London- and Tokyo-based artist Umi Ishihara, bringing together three recent films exploring precarity and collective life through personal memory and social realities.
exhibitions.venue_address: 235 Bowery, New York, NY 10002, United States
exhibitions.long_description:
It is one of three films in Ishihara's first US museum show, which brings back the New Museum's Screens Series. You move from a small Baptist church in Kitakyushu, where people who came through crime, homelessness and abuse stage a Passion Play in Gravity and Radiance, to Nocturnal Melody, 24 minutes with two Tokyo dancers backstage and on stage at a Shibuya gentleman's club.

Real congregants and dancers share the screen with fiction and animated animals, so expect neither straight documentary nor drama. Entry comes with general admission: $28 for adults, free for 18 and under, and pay what you wish on Thursdays from 7 to 9pm.

look_for.title: Thundergod's lightning club
look_for.text: Look for the underground club in an imaginary Japanese mountain village where only lightning-strike survivors perform, and the crabs the villagers keep running into.

look_for.title: The Passion Play in Gravity and Radiance
look_for.text: Members of a small Kitakyushu church, many with pasts of crime, homelessness or depression, act out the Passion in simple costumes and talk about how their lives changed.

look_for.title: Eri and Catalina in Nocturnal Melody
look_for.text: Two Tokyo dancers are filmed in dressing rooms and on stage at Madam Woo's club in Shibuya, partly in night vision, telling stories of childhood, dreams and politics.

look_for.title: Ishihara's night animals
look_for.text: In Nocturnal Melody's dream sequences, her stylised nocturnal animals roam Tokyo's streets at night, licking and clambering over each other.

exhibitions.title: Through Motion and Repose: Expanding the Walls 2026
exhibitions.description: Photography by seventeen teen artists from the Studio Museum's signature Expanding the Walls program, capturing New York's streets alongside intimate moments at home.
exhibitions.long_description:
Soriano is one of seventeen New York teenagers in this year's Expanding the Walls, the Studio Museum's photography program, and their prints run along one long wall. Some go close: Yoselyn Lucero's parents' nutrition store in the South Bronx, Isabella Amankwa-Jones's black-and-white portraits of people she recognises on 125th Street. Others blur streets and subways. The teens also chose two James Van Der Zee photographs from the collection to hang beside theirs, one at a time. Step outside afterwards and you are on Amankwa-Jones's street.

No critic has reviewed it. More photographs and each artist's statement are online at expandingthewalls.studiomuseum.org. Admission is pay-what-you-can ($16 suggested, $9 for students and seniors), free on Sundays and for under-16s, and Fridays run to 9pm.

look_for.title: Christopher Soriano, Suits at the Corner
look_for.text: Four jackets, rust, plum, black and camel, hang on hooks in a shop window, with street signs standing in front of the glass.

look_for.title: James Van Der Zee, Parade on Seventh Avenue in Harlem
look_for.text: Crowds line Seventh Avenue for a 1917 parade, picked by the teens from the museum's Van Der Zee collection; it alternates with his Capital Grill Restaurant, c. 1940.

look_for.title: Yoselyn Lucero, El Corazón del Negocio
look_for.text: Look for Nutrición Siempre Saludable, her parents' store in the South Bronx, and the family and neighbours who come through it.

look_for.title: Isabella Amankwa-Jones's 125th Street portraits
look_for.text: Formal black-and-white portraits of people of colour she recognises on 125th Street, the street the museum stands on.

exhibitions.title: Geometries
exhibitions.description: A group exhibition exploring geometry as an organizational principle, translating sources from city maps to West African textiles into a shared visual vocabulary spanning figuration and abstraction.
exhibitions.long_description:
Everything comes from the museum's collection: thirty artists, from Alma Thomas and Norman Lewis to Julie Mehretu, working with lines, shapes and the gaps between them. In Jack Whitten's Psychic Intersection you see raked wavy lines, a perfect circle and a black square near the centre that the label compares to a black hole. Shinique Smith tied a bale of clothes with twine and subtitled it (with Cookie Pants): the wash-and-fold bag, promoted to sculpture.

No critic has reviewed it yet. Admission is pay-what-you-can ($16 suggested for adults, $9 for seniors and students), free on Sundays and for anyone 16 and under, and Fridays run to 9pm.

look_for.title: James Little, Homage El-Shabazz (#10)
look_for.text: Four triangular canvases in one wooden frame form an X where they meet, in reds chosen for Malcolm X's sandy hair and his nickname, Detroit Red.

look_for.title: Steffani Jemison, Untitled (X)
look_for.text: A photograph of her Studio Museum residency window, taped in an X before Hurricane Sandy, printed on acetate so light and shadow play across the surface.

look_for.title: Torkwase Dyson, Of Line and Memory, Drawing Test 02
look_for.text: Look for the square and the triangle: Henry "Box" Brown's escape crate and the crawl space where Harriet Jacobs hid for seven years, turned into shapes.

look_for.title: Daniel LaRue Johnson, Nations
look_for.text: One black mass and one white, each capped with bright patches of colour, stand against cerulean blue and never quite meet.

look_for.title: Howard McCalebb, Frank Stella as Don Quixote in Defense of the Kaiser
look_for.text: The geometric painter Frank Stella recast as Don Quixote in rounded shapes and colour fields, with a joke equation in the lower left corner.

exhibitions.title: Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous
exhibitions.description: The first major New York presentation devoted to either artist in more than 20 years.
exhibitions.long_description:
Twelve chapters run from the 1930s to the end of both lives, with over 120 works from more than 80 lenders. Some galleries hang the two together, others give each their own. Critics disagree on the pairing. In Cultured, David Rimanelli said "He was better than her", and Julia Bryan-Wilson strongly disagreed. Krasner's The Seasons runs nearly 17 feet, the knot your earbuds become by the time the 6 train reaches Union Square.

Gallery 899 is a windowless corner of the second floor, and one preview report called it crowded. It's free with Museum admission and open until 9pm on Fridays and Saturdays. The Met is closed Wednesdays. It runs to 31 January 2027.
exhibitions.editors_pick: Lee Krasner and Jackson Pollock, wife and husband, in one Met exhibition. Neither has had a major New York show in over twenty years, so this is the first chance in a generation to judge them side by side.

look_for.title: The entrance video
look_for.text: A silent, collaged montage of film and photographs of the artists' Long Island cottage plays in a narrow hallway before the first painting.

look_for.title: Krasner's Bald Eagle collage
look_for.text: Cultured's critics say the show opens with her 1954-55 collages, made from spattered scraps of canvas from Pollock's studio.

look_for.title: Pollock's Full Fathom Five (1947)
look_for.text: Actual junk is embedded in the paint, which Cultured's panel singled out.

look_for.title: The Mosaic Table (1947)
look_for.text: A decorative table with concrete poured by Pollock. Rimanelli called it hideous but liked that it was included.

exhibitions.title: Art of Manga
exhibitions.description: East Coast debut of the first major Americas exhibition on manga as an art form, with more than 600 original drawings including Inuyasha, JoJo's Bizarre Adventure and ONE PIECE.
exhibitions.venue_address: 200 Eastern Parkway, Brooklyn, NY 11238, United States
exhibitions.long_description:
More than 600 original drawings, the genga that printed pages are made from, fill the first-floor Great Hall. An introduction to manga history leads to Chiba Tetsuya and Akatsuka Fujio, then eight artists get a section each, including Oda, Takahashi, Tagame and Taniguchi. The last section shows Shueisha Manga-Art Heritage prints. The galleries run right to left, like a volume, and Kinokuniya has put printed books in the middle for handling. Wear the wig: the 2 train to Eastern Parkway has seen worse.

Timed tickets start at $30 for adults and include general admission, with entry every 15 minutes from 11am and last entry at 5pm. The museum is open Wednesday to Sunday, 11am to 6pm. The $75 Manga Fan Pass covers two people for unlimited visits.
exhibitions.editors_pick: More than 600 original drawings: the hand-inked pages behind Inuyasha, JoJo's Bizarre Adventure and ONE PIECE. The first major show in the Americas to treat manga as art, with a companion collection show tracing 900 years of Japanese narrative pictures.

look_for.title: Araki's JoJo painting
look_for.text: A life-sized, 12-panel work made so the viewer can imagine being inside the JoJo's Bizarre Adventure landscape.

look_for.title: Chiba Tetsuya's last page of Ashita no Joe
look_for.text: Original final-page artwork of the boxing series, rarely exhibited outside Japan.

look_for.title: Taniguchi Jiro's self-portrait
look_for.text: An unfinished late self-portrait, lent outside Japan for the first time by his widow.

look_for.title: The Kinokuniya book section
look_for.text: Printed manga volumes you can pick up and read among the drawings they came from.

look_for.title: The Shueisha prints
look_for.text: The final section shows art prints of ONE PIECE, Rose of Versailles and BLEACH.

exhibitions.title: Manga Before Manga: Japanese Art from the Collection
exhibitions.description: Twenty-one works from the collection trace 900 years of Japanese narrative imagery behind modern manga; a companion to Art of Manga.
exhibitions.venue_address: 200 Eastern Parkway, Brooklyn, NY 11238, United States
exhibitions.long_description:
It is a Spotlight of 21 collection works in the first-floor Great Hall, which it shares with Art of Manga, and it is there as that show's backstory. You move from scroll to woodblock prints, illustrated books, a porcelain lion and an enamel plate, past heroes, lovers and supernatural beings. Kuniyoshi's boy wrestles a giant carp under a waterfall, and an 1887 Kawanabe Kyōsai book already has manga in its title. The Fujin plate has a Manhattan past: Herter Brothers fitted it into John Sloane's Fifth Avenue house in 1882.

It is small, so pair it with Art of Manga on one visit. Entry is included in general admission, pay what you can (suggested $20, free for 19 and under), Wednesday to Sunday, 11am to 6pm, through January 31.

look_for.title: Tale of the Wisteria Robe
look_for.text: A 15th-century handscroll in ink on mica-flecked paper, over 33 feet long, whose graphic devices the museum reads as early speech bubbles.

look_for.title: Kuniyoshi's Sakata Kaidōmaru
look_for.text: A well-muscled boy wrestles a giant carp under a waterfall, drawn with a see-through stream of water and scattering white spray.

look_for.title: The Fujin plate
look_for.text: Look for the wind god slinging a heavy bag of wind over his shoulders against swirling air, above birds and leaves on a turquoise ground.

look_for.title: Yoshitoshi's Matsunaga Hisahide
look_for.text: A warrior facing certain death throws down the treasured tea bowl his enemy wanted, so that nobody gets it.

exhibitions.title: The Bowery: Devil's Mile
exhibitions.description: The inaugural exhibition traces five centuries of the Bowery's history, from Lenape footpath through skid row to thriving arts community, examining the street as a site of ongoing reinvention.
exhibitions.venue_address: 235 Bowery, New York, NY 10002, United States
exhibitions.long_description:
The show runs in order: old maps and a marble milestone, Jacob Riis's flash photographs, Weegee and Berenice Abbott, then CBGB in the late 1970s. A small room plays Nan Goldin's The Ballad of Sexual Dependency, much of it shot in her Bowery loft, which Art in America's J. Hoberman calls the outstanding work here. You walk out of it straight into a wall of 28 portraits by Billy Sullivan.

Hoberman calls the show compact but says it "punches above its weight." He misses Lionel Rogosin's 1956 film On the Bowery; the only film here is a 1902 comedy loop. Admission is $28, free for 18 and under, and pay what you wish on Thursdays from 7 to 9pm, booked online.

look_for.title: The Lady Washington pump wagon
look_for.text: Look for the enameled 1836 fire engine of a volunteer company, the centerpiece of the first gallery among the dime-museum handbills.

look_for.title: The Five Points painting
look_for.text: An unknown artist's early 19th-century copy of George Catlin's crowded slum street scene, which upstages the stiff Peter Stuyvesant portrait beside it.

look_for.title: Martha Rosler's Bowery grid
look_for.text: Forty-five photographs of empty Bowery storefronts and bottle-strewn gutters, paired with slang words for being drunk instead of captions.

look_for.title: Nan Goldin's The Ballad of Sexual Dependency
look_for.text: A slideshow of candid portraits of friends, many shot in her Bowery loft, in a small room with its own soundtrack.

look_for.title: Brad Kahlhamer's Bowery Nation
look_for.text: In the final gallery, a 25-foot wooden plank on sawhorses carries 22 spidery birds and rows of kachina dolls made from found objects and refuse.

exhibitions.title: Diego Marcon: Arrivederci, Piggies!
exhibitions.description: The Italian artist's first solo New York museum show presents three recent films alongside the newly commissioned "Krapfen" (2025), blending horror, comedy, and animation to explore desire, memory, and perception.
exhibitions.venue_address: 235 Bowery, New York, NY 10002, United States
exhibitions.long_description:
You stand in one room where four films play at once on large screens side by side. In Ludwig, a boy sits alone in the dark, lit now and then by a candle or lightning. In Fritz, a boy hangs from a noose and can't die. The Parents' Room is an operetta sung by a father who has killed his family, and by his dead wife and children.

David Lê of The Arcades called The Parents' Room the best of the four and urged readers to go. The museum's Massimiliano Gioni warned it "can freak some people out." Entry is general admission: $28 for adults, free for 18 and under, pay what you wish Thursdays 7 to 9pm, booked online.

look_for.title: Krapfen
look_for.text: A child in a frenetic dance with four animated garments, gloves, a scarf, trousers and a jumper, to a song that keeps repeating the name of a jam doughnut.

look_for.title: The Parents' Room
look_for.text: It opens on a bird chirping at a window, then the father, in prosthetics that leave only eyes and mouth bare, sings of killing his family.

look_for.title: Ludwig
look_for.text: A young boy sits alone in darkness, visible only when a candle flickers or lightning flashes.

look_for.title: Fritz
look_for.text: A boy hangs from a noose, failing again and again to die, until his body suddenly reanimates.

exhibitions.title: Charles Burchfield: Elemental
exhibitions.description: Ten watercolors from the Whitney's collection, spanning 1916–1960, tracing Charles Burchfield's visionary, lifelong reverence for natural phenomena, from flowering meadows to dramatic storms.
exhibitions.long_description:
It is one of ten watercolors from the Whitney's own collection, made between 1916 and 1960, of meadows, storms and turning seasons. They are light-sensitive and rarely shown together, and the show marks 70 years since the Whitney's 1956 Burchfield retrospective. He worked big and slow: An April Mood is 54 inches wide, and Overhanging Cloud in July took him twelve years.

It hangs on the seventh floor, and the Whitney's audio guide has a stop on Overhanging Cloud in July. Admission is $30, $24 for seniors and students, and free for visitors 25 and under, on Friday nights from 5 to 10pm and on second Sundays. The Whitney is closed Tuesdays.

look_for.title: Cricket Chorus in the Arbor (1917)
look_for.text: Look for the crickets' hum drawn as repeated black patterns in a thick hedge at sunset, with deep shadows in front and sunlit clouds behind.

look_for.title: An April Mood (1946–55)
look_for.text: Clusters of three old maples under a dark sky Burchfield called an "April frown", with yellow-tipped growth just breaking through the winter ground.

look_for.title: Overhanging Cloud in July (1947–59)
look_for.text: A sheet about a metre tall with yellow dashes and lines across the sky, which the photographer James Welling reads as a force field of summer heat.

exhibitions.title: Designing the Gilded Age: Drawings from the Studios of Louis C. Tiffany
exhibitions.description: The dazzling stained-glass windows, lamps, mosaics, and interiors from Tiffany's studios began as drawings created by the many talented designers who worked there.
exhibitions.long_description:
The rest is mostly paper: nearly 120 watercolor designs, all from The Met's collection, for windows, lamps, mosaics and interiors commissioned from the mid-1880s to the 1920s. Finished windows, mosaics, enamels and lamps hang beside their drawings. The designers were the studio's staff, often émigrés and women such as Clara Driscoll and Agnes Northrop. You come for the name on the lamp and leave knowing who drew it.

It runs until 7 February in Galleries 691-693 at The Met Fifth Avenue, free with Museum admission. Members can see it from 9 to 10am on select weekend mornings.

look_for.title: Woman in a Pergola with Wisteria (1911)
look_for.text: Look for the Chrysler Museum's stained-glass window shown with its original wisteria transoms, which were found in an Arizona home.

look_for.title: The Poppy lampshade design
look_for.text: Clara Driscoll and Alice Gouvy's watercolor design, around 1900, for one of the studio's poppy lampshades.

look_for.title: First Presbyterian Church, Poughkeepsie
look_for.text: A watercolor and graphite design for the church's whole interior, drawn around 1906-08 on transparent paper.

exhibitions.title: Breaking the Mold: Brooklyn Museum at 200
exhibitions.description: Three chapters of longtime favorites and new standouts, bringing fresh narratives to the fore while exploring the collection's history and future evolution. Marks the Museum's bicentennial.
exhibitions.venue_address: 200 Eastern Parkway, Brooklyn, NY 11238, United States
exhibitions.long_description:
More than 220 objects fill much of the fourth floor in three chapters. Brooklyn Made runs from Delaware Lenape youth moccasins to Georgia O'Keeffe's Brooklyn Bridge, and its curator put a Coney Island carousel horse where it greets you as you walk in. Look for Fred McDarrah's Polar Bear Club swimmer: if you've promised yourself the New Year's Day plunge three Januaries running, he went for you. The other chapters trace the museum back to an apprentices' library and show the anniversary gifts.

Brooklyn Magazine called it the museum playing its hits. It's in general admission: $20 suggested, pay what you can at the desk, free for 19 and under. Joel Sternfeld's photographs of activist David Buckel's self-immolation in Prospect Park are hard viewing.

look_for.title: Jenny Holzer's HEAP
look_for.text: Seven LED signs cycle through truisms and inflammatory messages, and Time Out says they pull visitors in like moths to a flame.

look_for.title: Robert Frank's Coney Island, July 4, 1958
look_for.text: Photographs from a single Independence Day at the beach, which Time Out found unusually melancholy for the place.

look_for.title: Lafayette's cornerstone
look_for.text: The first stone of the Brooklyn Apprentices' Library, the museum's origin, laid by Lafayette while a young Walt Whitman watched.

look_for.title: Francis Guy's Winter Scene in Brooklyn
look_for.text: Snow on the rooftops and smoke curling from chimneys under a foggy grey sky, painted and acquired in 1846.

look_for.title: The Bechers' water towers
look_for.text: German artists Bernd and Hilla Becher's late-1970s photographs of the water towers on New York's rooftops.

exhibitions.title: David Hartt: Peripheries
exhibitions.description: Multidisciplinary artist David Hartt transforms John Vanderlyn's 19th-century painting Panoramic View of the Palace and Gardens of Versailles into a site-specific installation exploring place and perspective.
exhibitions.long_description:
David Hartt filmed from Versailles to the Boulevard Périphérique and through central Paris, looking for breaks in the landscape where 200 years of political change show. He also borrows from French New Wave film and Eugène Atget's photographs of the palace grounds, and Jeff Parker wrote the score. The screens complete the painting in places and cut into it in others, so where you stand changes what you see. Vanderlyn painted the canvas for a rotunda he built in City Hall Park; it didn't pay, and he toured a 165-foot painting for the rest of his life.

It's one painting and one film in one room, Gallery 735 of the American Wing, free with Museum admission, through February 7, 2027.

look_for.title: The 165-foot Versailles
look_for.text: Vanderlyn's oil wraps the whole gallery in the palace and its gardens, with the perspective adjusted to the curve of the wall.

look_for.title: Vanderlyn painting himself in
look_for.text: Look right of the Basin de Latone for the artist himself, painted into the scene pointing out Czar Alexander I and the King of Prussia.

look_for.title: The two transparent screens
look_for.text: Two large LED screens stand in the round gallery; you see the painting through them, and their film completes or breaks into the painted view.

look_for.title: Paris out to the Périphérique
look_for.text: Hartt's footage runs from Versailles to the ring road and through central Paris, focusing on spots where two centuries of political upheaval left marks.

exhibitions.title: Teresa Margolles
exhibitions.description: Trained as a forensic pathologist and photographer, Margolles examines transnational violence, with particular attention to the US-Mexico border, through work that traces disappearances, femicides and displacement and rethinks the memorial.
exhibitions.venue_address: 22-25 Jackson Avenue, Long Island City, NY 11101
exhibitions.long_description:
Margolles trained as a forensic pathologist, and this is her first large-scale US museum show: three decades of sculpture, photography and video across PS1's third-floor galleries, plus a new commission. The centrepiece, La promesa, is a barrier of rubble from a house a family abandoned in Ciudad Juárez. A 296-minute video follows volunteers scrubbing shooting sites across Dallas, with each victim's name and address on screen.

Santana describes her approach as "unsparing", and the subject throughout is border violence, disappearances and femicides. Entry is free, and La promesa is activated daily at 3pm. A companion piece, Aproximación al lugar de los hechos, drips water onto heated steel plates in Gallery 212 at MoMA in Manhattan.

look_for.title: La promesa (2012)
look_for.text: Tons of rubble from a house a family abandoned in Ciudad Juárez, built into a monumental barrier that the museum activates daily at 3pm.

look_for.title: Aire (2003)
look_for.text: Two humidifiers fill a room with vapour from water collected at sites of violence in New York.

look_for.title: El agua de la ciudad, Dallas (2016)
look_for.text: In a 296-minute video, volunteers scrub the sites of shootings across Dallas, each scene captioned with the victim's name, age and address.

look_for.title: La nieve (2015)
look_for.text: A man shovels snow at the Staten Island memorial to Eric Garner, who was killed by police in 2014.

look_for.title: Receipt (2020)
look_for.text: A Walmart receipt for ammunition, enlarged to poster size and stacked so you can take a copy with you.

exhibitions.title: Homeroom: Artists Against the Bomb
exhibitions.description: An international artistic campaign in support of the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, presenting posters, film, photography, sculpture and ephemera by artists including Regina José Galindo and Carlos Amorales, organized by Estudio Pedro Reyes and ICAN.
exhibitions.venue_address: 22-25 Jackson Avenue, Long Island City, NY 11101
exhibitions.long_description:
Estudio Pedro Reyes organised it with ICAN, the group that won the 2017 Nobel Peace Prize, in support of the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons. The Homeroom presentation spans posters, design, film, photography, literature, music, sculpture and ephemera, with work by Regina José Galindo, Carlos Amorales, Art & Language and Laura Anderson Barbata, among others. No published reviews yet, so this describes rather than judges.

Entry is free. PS1 is open Thursday to Monday, noon to 6pm (10am on Saturdays), and closed Tuesday and Wednesday. The show runs to 8 February 2027.
exhibitions.editors_pick: Posters, film, photography, sculpture, and ephemera from an international artists' campaign for the treaty banning nuclear weapons, with work by Regina José Galindo and Carlos Amorales.

exhibitions.title: Frederic Church in Jamaica
exhibitions.description: Over 60 oil and graphite sketches from Church's 1865 trip to Jamaica, documenting plant life and landscapes, drawn from Cooper Hewitt's collection of the artist's work.
exhibitions.long_description:
Church had just lost two young children to diphtheria when he and his wife, Isabel, went to Jamaica in April 1865. For five months he went out every day, on foot or on horseback, and drew what he found: tree ferns, thatch palms, a lizard, the Blue Mountains near Kingston, bamboo by moonlight.

More than 60 of those oil studies and pencil sketches are on view, from Cooper Hewitt's 2,000-plus Church sketches, the largest holding of his work anywhere. The curator says they have rarely, if ever, been shown. Some took moments and some took hours, and you can read his notes on the pencil ones. Around them sit period photographs, rare books, and the voices of Paul Bogle and George William Gordon, Black Jamaicans who took on the island's political tensions under British rule.

It marks 200 years since Church's birth. Museum admission covers it, under-18s are free, and it's pay what you wish from 5 to 6pm daily. The free Bloomberg Connects app has the curator's commentary.

look_for.title: Church's pencil notes
look_for.text: Look closely at the graphite sketches: Church annotated many of them with short notes the museum describes as both informative and poetic.

look_for.title: Period photographs of Jamaica
look_for.text: Reproductions of 1860s photographs, some collected by Church himself and some from the National Library of Jamaica, show the island he was drawing.

exhibitions.title: The Substitute
exhibitions.description: Alexandra Daisy Ginsberg's immersive video and sound installation digitally resurrects an extinct male Northern white rhino using AI and visual effects, questioning whether species resurrection is a justified answer to extinction.
exhibitions.long_description:
It isn't, which is the point. Sudan, the last male northern white rhino, died in March 2018, and scientists stored his DNA for possible de-extinction. Alexandra Daisy Ginsberg answered with this life-size projection, 5 metres wide: its behaviour comes from DeepMind research on AI agents, its sounds from rare footage of the last herd. You watch a species come back as a simulation while a second screen plots its path. Ginsberg's question: "Can we conscionably resurrect a species when we couldn't keep it alive in the first place?"

It's one work inside the Design Across Time collection display, so general admission covers it: a reduced $10 for adults during an upstairs gallery changeover, free for under-18s, pay what you wish 5 to 6pm daily.

look_for.title: The pixel rhino
look_for.text: Look for the rhino as a blur of brown and grey squares at the start of the loop, sharpening into a lifelike animal as it learns the white room.

look_for.title: The data screen
look_for.text: A second screen beside the projection plays the experiment's data, tracing the rhino's path and the development of grid cells as it learns its space.

look_for.title: The last herd's voices
look_for.text: Listen for the rhino's sounds, adapted from rare research footage of the final northern white rhino herd.

exhibitions.title: Brancusi: The Artist and His Studio
exhibitions.description: For the first time in decades, rarely lent sculptures leave Brancusi's Paris atelier (closed for renovation) to join MoMA's Brancusi collection, alongside his photographs, films, hand-carved furniture, tools and archival materials.
exhibitions.long_description:
Arriving in New York in 1926, Brancusi looked around and said: "Why, it is my studio. All these blocks, all these shapes to be shifted and juggled with, as the experiment grows and changes." The studio he meant, at the impasse Ronsin in Paris, is where he lived, worked and received clients from 1916 until his death.

Its contents went to France and are now the Atelier Brancusi, closed during the Centre Pompidou's renovation, which is why the sculptures are travelling. They fill the sixth floor in largely chronological order: Leda, Bird in Space, Fish, and different versions of Mlle Pogany and The Kiss. Many stand on his original hand-carved bases, beside carved wood furniture, tools, and his own photographs and films. Brancusi hand-carved the bases under his sculptures; your plant sits on a milk crate by the fire escape.

It runs to February 27, 2027, and is included with general admission, $30 for adults.
exhibitions.editors_pick: Brancusi treated his Paris studio as a work in itself and photographed his sculptures there rather than trust anyone else to. MoMA gathers rarely lent pieces from the atelier with those photographs, his films, furniture and tools.

look_for.title: Sculptures on their original bases
look_for.text: Works stand on Brancusi's own hand-carved wood and stone bases, which the museum treats as being as carefully formed as the sculptures they hold.

look_for.title: Three versions each of The Kiss and Mlle Pogany
look_for.text: Versions dated between 1912 and 1940 hang together, showing one motif recurring in different materials and configurations.

look_for.title: Brancusi's own films
look_for.text: Films he made show his mobile sculptures in motion.

look_for.title: Studio photographs
look_for.text: Photographs he took himself record how the sculptures were rearranged in the studio over four decades.

look_for.title: Carved wood furniture
look_for.text: Furniture he carved sits among the sculptures, blurring the line between support, domestic object and artwork.

exhibitions.title: Dreams of This Future: The Collection of Peggy Cooper Cafritz
exhibitions.description: The first exhibition to tell the story of arts advocate Peggy Cooper Cafritz as a collector, drawing on her bequest of over 200 artists of African descent across multiple media.
exhibitions.long_description:
What hangs here is a slice of the 400-plus works she left the Studio Museum: nearly fifty artists, from Kerry James Marshall and Wangechi Mutu to former students of the DC public arts high school she cofounded. You read her voice on every wall: the quotes all come from her own book. Rozeal.'s portrait on a Louis Vuitton suitcase stood in her foyer to greet guests. Most New Yorkers greet theirs with a shoe rack.

No critic has reviewed it yet. Some works are hard going: Njena Surae Jarvis hangs cast body parts from cords and chains that recall lynching. Admission is pay-what-you-can ($16 suggested), free on Sundays and for anyone 16 and under, and Fridays run to 9pm.

look_for.title: Sanford Biggers, Jocko
look_for.text: Three chrome-plated bronze lawn jockeys, partly melted, one of the few pieces that came through the 2009 fire at Cafritz's house.

look_for.title: Rozeal., Dave, Dove
look_for.text: A man's portrait painted onto a Louis Vuitton suitcase, the LV pattern picked out in blue; it sat in Cafritz's foyer to welcome guests.

look_for.title: Hassan Hajjaj, Romancia
look_for.text: A figure poses on a moped named Romancia against bright blue, framed by 46 chicken bouillon boxes laid out like Moroccan zellige tiles.

look_for.title: Hank Willis Thomas, Basketball and Chain
look_for.text: A man in Nike sneakers leaps up and out of the frame, his ankles chained to a basketball, shot like a sleek minimalist ad.

look_for.title: Simone Leigh, No Face (Black)
look_for.text: A featureless Black female face in terracotta and porcelain, its edge ringed with tiny rosettes Leigh rolled by hand from bits of clay.

exhibitions.title: Jakob Kudsk Steensen: Wetland
exhibitions.description: Digital installation Berl-Berl reimagines Berlin's lost wetlands as a singing, digital swamp, blending ecological research, Slavic folklore and game-engine technology to explore human and more-than-human worlds.
exhibitions.long_description:
It is the show's only work, and it runs live: image and sound are computed in real time, so no pass repeats. Steensen spent months in Berlin's remaining wetlands with the Museum für Naturkunde, scanning soils, plants and currents with macro photogrammetry. You stand among wall-spanning screens while altered field recordings of amphibians mix with Arca's voice and Sorbian and Slavic songs. Berl-Berl opened in 2021 at Halle am Berghain and has changed with each stop since.

Time Out placed it between art installation and "extremely sophisticated nature documentary." It fills the Agnes Gund Garden Lobby on Floor 1 until March 7, 2027, and admission is free. Berlin named itself after its swamp; New York's still turns up on subway platforms after a hard rain.

look_for.title: Triglav as a giant tree
look_for.text: The three-headed god of Slavic folklore appears in the MoMA version of the swamp as a huge tree.

look_for.title: Swamp soil at giant scale
look_for.text: Macro photogrammetry blows up the microscopic textures of Berlin wetland soils, plants and currents across wall-spanning screens.

look_for.title: Arca and the amphibians
look_for.text: Digitally altered field recordings of amphibians and river rhythms are mixed with Arca's vocals and songs from Sorbian and Slavic traditions.

look_for.title: The insect's-eye view
look_for.text: The viewpoint shifts from a view of the whole marsh to a fragmented, insect-like perspective, and the real-time simulation never plays the same pass twice.

good_for: [Where to see Jakob Kudsk Steensen now →](https://www.musa.guide/en/discover/artists/jakob-kudsk-steensen)

exhibitions.title: Taryn Simon | Father Country I Do Love You
exhibitions.description: A major new commission premieres never-before-seen photographs, text, video, and sculpture in a single interactive installation spiraling through the entire rotunda.
exhibitions.venue_address: 1071 Fifth Avenue, New York, NY 10128, United States
exhibitions.long_description:
It is one of 42 chapters winding up the rotunda, the first time the Guggenheim has given the whole rotunda to one new body of work by a photography-based artist. Simon spent nearly a decade tracing the career of one unnamed federal agent, which touched the Marion Barry sting and the Nairobi embassy bombing. Forty-two chapters spiralling up one ramp is your 1am Wikipedia rabbit hole made physical, minus the phone at 4%.

Critics were split. Ostrow found the route "stubbornly linear" and the signage "ill-considered", while Aruna D'Souza in Hyperallergic argued that injustice here "seems purely systemic, not the result of individuals behaving badly". Plan to read. Admission is $30, and the museum is open daily 10:30am to 5:30pm.
exhibitions.editors_pick: Taryn Simon fills the whole rotunda with one federal agent's career, told in 42 chapters up Wright's ramp. Simon builds her work from photographs, documents and text, so plan on reading as much as looking.

look_for.title: The marble cabinet
look_for.text: Crank the handle and marbles run down a track while a screen plays an elderly man narrating slides.

look_for.title: Jodie Foster's fingerprinting drill
look_for.text: Foster reenacts a color-coded fingerprinting exercise from her preparation for The Silence of the Lambs.

look_for.title: Paul Ames and the auction lots
look_for.text: Portraits of Paul Ames, son of the convicted spy Aldrich Ames, hang beside photographs of confiscated items sold at government auction.

look_for.title: Letters from Lee Boyd Malvo
look_for.text: Correspondence and artwork from the incarcerated sniper, part of the agent's wider paper trail.

look_for.title: The teak-panelled introduction
look_for.text: Text panels set against teak paneling, a replica of a Bangkok spy's living room, recount her father's stories and her meeting with the agent.

exhibitions.title: New York Fashion at PS1, 1980–1984
exhibitions.description: Archive material and partial reconstructions of the fashion installations curator Hollywood Di Russo staged at PS1 with Julio, Charles James, Willi Smith and Betsey Johnson.
exhibitions.venue_address: 22-25 Jackson Avenue, Long Island City, NY 11101
exhibitions.long_description:
One film here is cut from more than 20 hours of footage of Charles James talking in his studio at the Chelsea Hotel, shot in 1978. The other, Made in New York, is a rarely screened 1984 WilliWear production with cameos from Willi Smith, Bill T. Jones and Jenny Holzer.

Between 1980 and 1984 the stylist Hollywood Di Russo staged ten fashion shows at PS1, on the premise that fashion "undeniably influences the way that we see." She skipped the usual costume display: clothes were pinned to walls, stuffed and hung salon-style, or stiffened in plaster and laid on the floor. Back then, clothes on the floor was a curatorial position, not a bedroom you hadn't tidied. You get original pieces and partial reconstructions of four of those shows, by Julio Espada, Charles James, Willi Smith and Betsey Johnson, plus archive photographs.

Entry is free; tickets can be reserved online. It opens on 5 November, and the Open House on 7 November includes a 2pm talk, A Fashion Alternative.

look_for.title: The Charles James film
look_for.text: A film compiled from more than 20 hours of footage of the couturier talking in his Chelsea Hotel studio, shot in 1978 by Anton Perich and R. Couri Hay.

look_for.title: Made in New York (Les Levine, 1984)
look_for.text: A rarely screened WilliWear film with cameos from Willi Smith, Bill T. Jones and Arnie Zane, Jenny Holzer and Arman.

exhibitions.title: Hard Art
exhibitions.description: A major exhibition examining the legacy of abstract painting by Black artists in the US from 1969 to today, featuring over forty artists across three generations.
exhibitions.venue_address: 22-25 Jackson Avenue, Long Island City, NY 11101
exhibitions.long_description:
In 1980 PS1 hung a show called Afro-American Abstraction, and Lorraine O'Grady answered it with a performance that demanded "BLACK ART MUST TAKE MORE RISKS!!!" Forty-six years later, in the same building, this show takes her demand as its starting point.

It gathers more than forty artists across three generations. Paintings by artists who came up in the 1970s, such as Frank Bowling, Ed Clark and Sam Gilliam, hang alongside recent sculpture, video and sound, and several works come straight from landmark shows: The DeLuxe Show (1971), whose curator Peter Bradley supplied the title, and PS1's own 1980 exhibition. You reach a double-height gallery filled end to end by a freestanding structure Torkwase Dyson built for it.

Entry is free, and tickets can be reserved online. PS1 is open Thursday to Monday, noon to 6pm, and from 10am on Saturdays. The Open House on 7 November includes a talk revisiting the 1980 show, and the Bloomberg Connects app carries the wall text and artists' audio.
exhibitions.editors_pick: Abstract painting by Black artists in the United States from 1969 to today, more than 40 of them across three generations. It hangs in MoMA's former schoolhouse in Queens, where entry is now free.

look_for.title: Torkwase Dyson's new environment
look_for.text: A newly commissioned freestanding architectural structure that spans the whole of PS1's double-height gallery.

look_for.title: Lorraine O'Grady, Landscape (Western Hemisphere)
look_for.text: An 18-minute video of the artist's hair in close-up, blown by fans until it reads as a shifting landscape, over a soundtrack of birds, insects, wind and city noise.

look_for.title: Maren Hassinger, The Veil Between Us
look_for.text: Look for newspapers twisted and knotted into a veil, held together with twine, wire, rope and steel.

exhibitions.title: Masao Gozu: Windows and Bars
exhibitions.description: First US museum show of Masao Gozu: photographs from the 1970s to today, from his Windows series of tenement residents and the Harry's Bar series, with recent returns to the same sites.
exhibitions.venue_address: 22-25 Jackson Avenue, Long Island City, NY 11101
exhibitions.long_description:
From 1976 to 1981, Masao Gozu kept photographing the front window of Harry's Bar at 98 Bowery, taking a picture each time a customer gazed out of its left side. Twelve of those frames are here. When the bar closed, he asked to buy the window itself and was turned down. Plenty of New Yorkers pay extra rent for a window; he wanted to own one outright.

That refusal started his sculptures. Gozu arrived in the 1970s with no photography training and shot apartment windows from the street, mostly in immigrant neighbourhoods from Chinatown to Crown Heights, each squared up in the darkroom to face you flat. Over 40 works run from 1972 to now, and you see old frames beside his recent returns to the same addresses.

This is his first US museum show, and nobody has reviewed it yet. Entry is free, with tickets reservable online. It opens on 5 November, and the 7 November Open House includes a workshop, Looking Out / Looking In.

look_for.title: Harry's Bar, 98 Bowery
look_for.text: Twelve shots of the same bar window between 1976 and 1981, each taken the moment a customer gazed out of its left side.

look_for.title: The 25th Street window (1992)
look_for.text: A window salvaged from a torn-down facade on 25th Street, rebuilt at quarter scale from brick, lintel and frame Gozu cut down himself.

look_for.title: Sunset between the towers
look_for.text: Three large colour photographs of windows Gozu installed around New York and New Jersey, placed so the sun set between the World Trade Center towers.

look_for.title: Mott Street, then and now
look_for.text: Look for Chinatown's Mott Street windows shot in 1972, hung with Gozu's recent photographs of the same site.

exhibitions.title: Kapwani Kiwanga: BLEED
exhibitions.description: A site-specific installation by Kapwani Kiwanga reworking the quilting "flying geese" pattern in natural dyes, evoking the Underground Railroad and histories of Black resistance.
exhibitions.long_description:
You stand in front of a dappled black made by oxidising pigment with salt water from the Atlantic, indigo for the blue swells, and a red oval dyed with pokeberries, a toxic North American fruit. The berries are for Delphy, a Black woman accused in 1816 of poisoning her enslaver with them. Kiwanga used fugitive dyes, colours that can change over time, so the wall keeps a record of its own run.

It is one work in one room, and no critic has reviewed it yet. Entry is pay-what-you-can ($16 suggested), free on Sundays and for anyone 16 and under, and Fridays run to 9pm.

look_for.title: The pokeberry oval
look_for.text: A red oval floats in the indigo, dyed with pokeberries for Delphy, accused in 1816 of poisoning her enslaver with the fruit.

look_for.title: The Atlantic black
look_for.text: The dappled black wave along the bottom was made by oxidising pigment with salt water collected from the Atlantic Ocean.

look_for.title: The flying geese in indigo
look_for.text: Look closely at the blue: it is pieced from triangles, the quilt motif said to point the way north, dyed with indigo, a plantation crop of the South.

exhibitions.title: Donald Moffett: IMPEACH
exhibitions.description: An immersive sound installation built around Representative John Lewis's speech on the floor of the US House during the December 1998 impeachment debate.
exhibitions.venue_address: 200 Eastern Parkway, Brooklyn, NY 11238, United States
exhibitions.long_description:
There is nothing to look at. Moffett made the piece in 2006 from a Library of Congress recording, and it is only speakers and a media player running a loop of 2 minutes 20 seconds. You step in and get Lewis's voice, the echo of applause and that gavel. Brooklyn and the Virginia Museum of Fine Arts bought it together in 2018, and Lewis went to hear it himself in Richmond in 2019.

It is on the 5th floor, included in general admission, and part of the museum's Drawing America: US@250 season. More of Moffett's work is in Common Sense, on until 8 November.

look_for.title: The gavel
look_for.text: Listen for the Judiciary Committee chairman's gavel coming down as he tries to silence Lewis mid-speech.

look_for.title: The storm story
look_for.text: Lewis recounts surviving a devastating storm and turns it into a plea to stay together as one house and one family.

look_for.title: The applause
look_for.text: Moffett keeps the echoes of applause from the House floor in the recording, around Lewis's voice.

exhibitions.title: Cézanne to Modigliani: Gifts of Modern Art from the Pearlman Collection
exhibitions.description: More than 50 modern European works by Cézanne, Modigliani, Degas, Gauguin, Toulouse-Lautrec and Soutine, from the Henry and Rose Pearlman Collection gift.
exhibitions.venue_address: 200 Eastern Parkway, Brooklyn, NY 11238, United States
exhibitions.long_description:
More than 50 works fill the fourth floor of the Schapiro Wing. The Pearlmans bought Cézanne in depth, landscapes and a cache of watercolors, alongside Degas, Gauguin, Manet and Van Gogh. Letters, photographs and portraits of Henry by Kokoschka and Lipchitz tell the couple's story: he grew up in Park Slope, Rose arrived from Minsk aged four. After fifty years on loan to Princeton, the collection now hangs a short walk from where he grew up.

It's the collection's last full tour. Entry is included in general admission, untimed and pay what you can (suggested $20, free for 19 and under), through April 18, 2027.

look_for.title: Soutine's View of Céret
look_for.text: The painting that started the collection opens the show: a town in southern France, paint applied as if by trowel and swirled into a vortex.

look_for.title: Toulouse-Lautrec's The Sacred Grove
look_for.text: A 12-foot send-up of a prize-winning Puvis de Chavannes, with a clock on the classical portico, a boy eating bread, and Lautrec himself urinating in the grove.

look_for.title: Modigliani's Jean Cocteau
look_for.text: Cocteau, proud of his straight nose, got painted with a bump; he bought the portrait for 5 francs, then left it behind because he couldn't afford a taxi home.

look_for.title: Van Gogh's Tarascon Stagecoach
look_for.text: Green carriages before a thickly painted yellow wall in Arles, done in one October afternoon in 1888; look between the wheel spokes, where bare canvas shows.

exhibitions.title: Taking Back Our Space: Photographic Perspectives
exhibitions.description: Marianne Wex's 1970s feminist photo survey of gendered body language is shown alongside contemporary artists Nona Faustine, Martine Gutierrez, K8 Hardy, Yuki Kihara, Joiri Minaya, Paulina Olowska, and Wendy Red Star, reappraising bodies in public space.
exhibitions.long_description:
MoMA owns the whole project, and here it shares a gallery with seven contemporary artists, each shown at MoMA for the first time. You turn from Wex's sorted strangers to K8 Hardy in wigs and costumes across fifty prints, sampling the poses Wex filed as male or female. Wex had a panel category for how people sit decades before the MTA printed posters about it.

No major critic has reviewed it yet, so take it as the curators' argument: a 1970s system, retested on race, colonialism and Indigenous sovereignty. It's in the second-floor Paul J. Sachs Galleries until May 2, 2027.

look_for.title: Martine Gutierrez, Body En Thrall
look_for.text: Posed like a Hollywood starlet, Gutierrez wraps her legs around a mannequin and stares at the camera, flipping the dynamics of Wex's "Possessive Holds" panels.

look_for.title: Nona Faustine at the Tweed Courthouse
look_for.text: Nude except for white heels, Faustine braces against a marble column of the downtown Manhattan courthouse, a few steps from the African Burial Ground.

look_for.title: Yuki Kihara's fa'afafine after Gauguin
look_for.text: Three photographs restage Gauguin's Polynesian paintings with fa'afafine models who hold your gaze, in front of waterfalls, lush plants and a wallpaper of Samoa's Aleipata islands.

look_for.title: Joiri Minaya, Wake
look_for.text: Minaya peels off a tropical-print bodysuit while waves from a tourist postcard are laid over her, so she half disappears into the background.

look_for.title: Wendy Red Star's Accession collages
look_for.text: Ten collages layer 1930s Denver Art Museum catalogue drawings of Apsáalooke objects with her own photographs from the Crow Fair.

exhibitions.title: Roy Lichtenstein: Like New
exhibitions.description: A comprehensive retrospective of roughly 130 works spanning the 1940s through the 1990s, tracing how Roy Lichtenstein transformed mass-culture imagery into iconic Pop art while probing duplication and the circulation of images across media.
exhibitions.long_description:
You start by walking the nearly 96-foot Greene Street Mural, one of four rebuilt murals, to Image Duplicator, a pair of bulging comic-book eyes. Then roughly 130 works fill the fifth floor, including Look Mickey and Drowning Girl. The curators frame it around copying, and Lawler, Pettibone and Sturtevant, who each copied him in turn, hang alongside. The title comes from a 1962 canvas, and it is also the two words on every resale listing you have ever scrolled past.

Wallpaper called it "revelatory and snappy". ARTnews found it stylish rather than a rethink, peaking at the Rouen Cathedral paintings, and suggested skimming the last third.
