Admission is $30, free for visitors 25 and under, and the Whitney recommends booking ahead. Fridays run until 10pm, free from 5pm.
exhibitions.editors_pick: About 130 works from the 1940s to the 1990s, with the paintings from his 1962 debut at Leo Castelli hung together again. A full retrospective, and the one to see if you only know the comic-strip canvases.

look_for.title: The 1962 Castelli debut, reunited
look_for.text: All eight paintings from Lichtenstein's first Pop-style show hang in their original arrangement, the first time they have been together since.

look_for.title: Greene Street Mural, rebuilt
look_for.text: A nearly 96-foot wall of his signature brushstrokes and benday dots opens the show, with vitrines of drawings, maquettes and Polaroids set into it.

look_for.title: The Mirrors room
look_for.text: A rounded, silver-walled room ringed with eight Mirror canvases from 1969 to 1972, dotted circles of glass that reflect nothing, the most ever shown together in a retrospective.

look_for.title: Lawler, Pettibone and Sturtevant
look_for.text: Three artists who built work out of copying Lichtenstein hang beside the paintings they copied.

look_for.title: Girl in Window, outdoors
look_for.text: Alex Da Corte and his studio hand-painted a 32-foot-tall Girl in Window on the Whitney's facade, so part of the show can be seen without going in.

exhibitions.title: Graphic Devotions: Late Medieval European Blockbooks
exhibitions.description: Blockbooks from 1450–80, when woodblock-printed books competed with manuscripts and typeset books, including a rare Ars moriendi, from the largest US collection of blockbooks.
exhibitions.long_description:
On every page of a blockbook, the words and the picture were cut into the same block of wood and printed together. They are often called "medieval graphic novels", and they were the first print-on-demand books in the West. They appeared around 1450 and had largely died out by 1480.

For those thirty years they competed with handwritten manuscripts and with books set in movable type, and lost: carving a page in wood was slower than setting it. The centrepiece is an Ars moriendi, a guide to dying well, printed in the Netherlands around 1467 to 1469. Pierpont Morgan bought nine of its 24 leaves in 1902, and the museum bought the other fifteen from a private collection in 2022, so you are looking at the only known complete copy.

The Morgan holds the largest blockbook collection in the United States, and curator John McQuillen's catalogue is a census of every blockbook or fragment in US collections. The Morgan stays open until 8pm on Fridays.

look_for.title: The reunited Ars moriendi (c. 1467-69)
look_for.text: A woodcut guide to dying well, shown whole: nine leaves Pierpont Morgan bought in 1902 rejoined by fifteen the museum bought in 2022, the only known complete copy.

exhibitions.title: Flip Sides: Seeing Korean Art Anew
exhibitions.description: Treasured Korean objects are turned around to reveal their interiors, reverses, and hidden details, offering a fuller view of each work's form across two rotations.
exhibitions.long_description:
It's one gallery, 233, with about 50 Korean objects from the Met's own collection, more than half on view for the first time. Things are turned so you see the side usually kept from you: a celadon box left open to show the swirled clay at its rim, the stamp faces of bronze seals, bowls whose incised waves sit inside. If you turn mugs over in shops to read the bottom, this is a whole gallery built on that habit.

It's included with Met admission. Some works change when the second rotation opens on October 31, 2026, and Met Expert Talks on the show run November 5, February 2 and May 4, at 3pm.

look_for.title: Kashyapa, the smiling monk
look_for.text: A relaxed, smiling wooden figure of the Buddha's eldest disciple, hollowed for offerings; a scroll found inside dates him to 1700.

look_for.title: The openwork peony jar
look_for.text: Four large peonies with twisting branches form a porcelain lattice, and an X-ray scan shows a second vessel concealed inside.

look_for.title: The mirror with a Buddha on its face
look_for.text: Unlike the other bronze mirrors here, its image is on the reflective side: Amitabha and two bodhisattvas on lotuses, enlarged on the case glass.

look_for.title: The marbled celadon box
look_for.text: A three-inch Goryeo box displayed open, so you can see the spiral of two blended clays at the rim under the green glaze.

look_for.title: The bird-shaped burial vessel
look_for.text: A 3rd-century earthenware bird with a 'mohawk'; its scan shows the head was made separately and a metal staple reinforces the base.

exhibitions.title: Roy Lichtenstein: 1997
exhibitions.description: A focused show of rarely seen works from the final year of the Pop artist's life, including prints, photographs and sculptural maquettes alongside studies for unrealized projects, revealing his late-career experimentation.
exhibitions.long_description:
The rest of this third-floor show is studies rather than finished pictures: two pyramids of cut paper, tape and acrylic on foamcore, a sketch for a chapel mural that was never built, and two mirrored panels for a Bellagio hotel mural. The Whitney notes his palette was widening to mint green, turquoise, coral and cyan, and the heavy black outlines were going. Paper folded onto foamcore to pass for solid is also how StreetEasy photos make a studio read as a loft.

Whitehot Magazine's Kurt Cole Eidsvig found a show to be seen and enjoyed in its own right. For finished Pop paintings, Like New on the fifth floor is the one. Admission is $30, free for visitors 25 and under, and the Whitney is open until 10pm on Fridays.
exhibitions.editors_pick: Prints, photographs, sculptural maquettes, and studies for projects he never realized, all from 1997, the last year of Lichtenstein's life. Most of it is rarely shown.

look_for.title: Brushstroke Still Life with Box
look_for.text: An empty vase and an empty box, with a bare white strip down the left edge where the obliterating brushstroke was meant to be painted. A 1996 study hangs with it.

look_for.title: Wall Pyramid (Model) and Pyramid (Maquette)
look_for.text: Tent-like pyramids of cut painted and printed paper, taped onto foamcore. The solid look is an illusion of folded surfaces, shown against a study of a suburban house.

look_for.title: Bellagio Hotel Mural: Still Life with Reclining Nude (Study)
look_for.text: Two mirrored panels: one a comic-book-style reclining nude, the other echoing an ancient statue, with a man holding an artist's palette.

look_for.title: Chapel of the Eucharist Mural (Study)
look_for.text: Leonardo's Last Supper table with no figures at it, and a flash of light above it that the critic called a visual POP.

exhibitions.title: Michael Richards: Free F’All
exhibitions.description: Michael Richards's sculpture of a pilot pierced with nails commemorates the Tuskegee Airmen, the US Air Force's first Black unit.
exhibitions.venue_address: 200 Eastern Parkway, Brooklyn, NY 11238, United States
exhibitions.long_description:
It is one sculpture, the only Richards in the museum's collection, from a series he spent nearly ten years on about the Tuskegee Airmen, Black pilots who fought in World War II in a segregated military. The museum reads the nails two ways: as the Kongolese nkisi nkondi, a guardian figure woken by each nail, and as Saint Sebastian's arrows. Richards died on September 11, 2001, in his North Tower studio.

It stands in the first-floor Rubin Lobby, so see it on the way to a bigger show. It is included in general admission, pay what you can (suggested $20, free for 19 and under), through June 6, 2027.

look_for.title: The nails
look_for.text: Dozens of them pierce the figure from collarbone to mid-thigh, down the arms and through the hands and feet, like a crucifixion.

look_for.title: The pilot's gear
look_for.text: Look for the aviator's flight cap, goggles and parachute backpack on a figure whose eyes are closed and arms pinned to his sides.

look_for.title: The rust-coloured surface
look_for.text: Fiberglass and resin coated in iron oxide, cast from a mold Richards made of his own body, with a slight bend in the right knee.

exhibitions.title: The Genesis Facade Commission: Liu Wei, Speculation
exhibitions.description: Beijing-based artist Liu Wei (born 1972) inspires visitors to ponder cycles of rupture and resistance for the 2026 Genesis Facade Commission.
exhibitions.long_description:
The works are named for physical constants (Λ, G, c, h). The two flanking the entrance are monumental, the outer two more delicate, all built from fiberglass, steel, bronze and bovine rawhide. Liu Wei says: "Our reality is a puzzle built by time. I want to answer it with a puzzle." A hand reaching up from a black sphere is you gripping the pole on the 6 at 86th Street when the driver brakes.

This is Liu Wei's first major US project. It's free to view from Fifth Avenue until June 8, 2027.
exhibitions.editors_pick: Beijing-based Liu Wei takes over the Met's Fifth Avenue facade with a work about cycles of rupture and resistance, free to see from the street.

look_for.title: Speculation / Λ
look_for.text: A black sphere holds up a hand reaching skyward, as if trapped in a ruin of bone tissue.

look_for.title: Speculation / G
look_for.text: An outstretched hand lies at the base of a tower of protruding nails, rawhide and layered geometric metal cutouts.

look_for.title: Speculation / c
look_for.text: One side reads as a premodern saint carved from rock and melted into a scream, the other side has an index finger pointing up.

look_for.title: Speculation / h
look_for.text: A heart-shaped form with grafted fingers that nearly clutch the organ.

exhibitions.title: Full Disclosure: The Edge of Information Design
exhibitions.description: MoMA's first exhibition devoted entirely to information design, presenting 30 works of digital and analog design (including six new acquisitions) that explore how designers help visualize and shape our understanding of complex data.
exhibitions.long_description:
About 30 works fill a windowed gallery on MoMA's ground floor, all but one from the collection. They range from new prints extending W.E.B. Du Bois's 1900 data portraits to New York Times 3D reconstructions of Notre Dame and Tulsa's Greenwood neighborhood, and Kate Crawford and Vladan Joler's Calculating Empires covers three walls of a side room. You move between screens you can work through and Dear Data, hand-drawn postcards two designers mailed each other across the Atlantic. Curator Paola Antonelli wants you to leave reading every chart with "more critical eyes."

Come if you make or read charts. The catch is Calculating Empires, dense on purpose: Galerie's writer argues its density "is the argument." It's included with admission ($30 adults, 16 and under free) until June 13, 2027.

look_for.title: Warming Stripes
look_for.text: The first piece in the show: one stripe per year since 1850, sliding from deep blue to bright red as the global average temperature climbs.

look_for.title: Calculating Empires
look_for.text: Icons and text cover three walls of a side room, tracing technology and power from the Gutenberg press to now.

look_for.title: Dear Data postcards
look_for.text: Ink-and-pencil postcards Giorgia Lupi and Stefanie Posavec sent between New York and London, each one a hand-drawn chart of a week in their lives.

look_for.title: The Synthetic Memories Archive
look_for.text: AI-generated pictures of memories that were never photographed hang on the wall, with the real people's prompt texts printed underneath.

look_for.title: Two Sides of the Same Coin
look_for.text: A model mapping human-associated microbes on one side and more than 12,000 years of global land use on the other.

exhibitions.title: Nilima Sheikh: Fractured Skies
exhibitions.description: A survey of painter Nilima Sheikh's five-decade practice, tracing her engagement with Kashmir through narrative scroll paintings including a new, site-responsive series debuting at MoMA.
exhibitions.long_description:
This is Sheikh's first solo show in New York. Five double-sided scrolls from Each Night Put Kashmir in Your Dreams hang mid-gallery, each 12 by 6 feet, so you walk around each one to read its other side. Paintings on paper about Kashmir's nomadic Bakarwal communities line the walls. Then come the ten new scrolls of Shahid (Witness), made for this room: burned and flooded land below, grey skies with blood-red horizons above.

It is slow, text-heavy painting, threaded with poetry by Agha Shahid Ali, and the subject is violence, including two panels on the 2018 attack on Asifa, an eight-year-old Bakarwal girl. A gallery handout decodes We Must Bear. It runs until June 13, 2027, included with admission ($30 adults, 16 and under free).

look_for.title: The weeping woman in We Must Bear
look_for.text: Look at the scroll's lower left: a kneeling woman cries red tears over a lozenge in her lap, with a stencilled child in a cradle behind her.

look_for.title: The figure carrying a body uphill
look_for.text: At the centre of We Must Bear, a figure struggles up a slope under a lifeless body, a pose Sheikh took from a Safavid painting of Cain and Abel.

look_for.title: The graves along the Line of Control
look_for.text: Repeating octagonal lozenges stand for anonymous border graves, some overlaid with flowers cut in Sanjhi paper stencils made with artisans in Mathura.

look_for.title: The skies of Shahid (Witness)
look_for.text: Across ten new scrolls, fire and flood fill the lower registers while otherworldly beings watch from above and birds fly toward paler, bluer skies.

look_for.title: The stencilled words in Home, Land 4
look_for.text: Bakarwal voices are lettered across the landscape: "We are living in forests for hundreds of years and now we are being termed as illegal occupants."

exhibitions.title: Hopi Kachina Dolls: Blessings for a Balanced World
exhibitions.description: The first exhibition to examine the Hopi kachina doll tradition from the perspective of the women and girls who receive them, presented at the Center for Feminist Art.
exhibitions.venue_address: 200 Eastern Parkway, Brooklyn, NY 11238, United States
exhibitions.long_description:
Fifty-three tithu, carved from cottonwood and painted, are among more than 120 works from the 19th century to now. They represent Katsinam, spirits who bring rain to the Hopi in arid northeastern Arizona, and they are given mainly to girls and women. Sections follow the corn-grinding ceremony, marriage and the summer Butterfly Dance. The last holds thirty pots, baskets and pieces of jewelry by Hopi women, and a video of six artists.

It fills the Center for Feminist Art on the 4th floor and is included in general admission: pay what you can at the desk (suggested $20, free for 19 and under). The audio guide is on Bloomberg Connects. It runs through June 27, 2027.

look_for.title: Henry Shelton's Mudhead
look_for.text: Look for a Kooyemsi doll carved from cottonwood root in the 1960s and finished with feathers, yarn and iron.

look_for.title: Shelton's Father Sun
look_for.text: Taawa, the Father Sun, carved by the same hand and dressed in silver discs, fur, beads and silk ribbon.

look_for.title: The Butterfly Dance ensembles
look_for.text: A boy's historical kilt whitened with Hopi clay beside a ribbon shirt, and a girl's kopatsoki tablita headdress with a handmade dress and cape.

look_for.title: The groom's wedding plaque
look_for.text: A hahawpi given to the groom, shown with photographs of a Hopi bride's wedding attire.

look_for.title: Verma Nequatewa's Hopi Maiden Pendant
look_for.text: A 1997 pendant in 14-karat gold, set with opal, fossilized ivory, coral, sugilite and turquoise.

exhibitions.title: Tapa: Art of the Gift in Polynesia
exhibitions.description: 19th-century bark cloth tapa from Fiji, Samoa and Futuna, plus a Niuean hiapo on loan from Te Papa, shown as ceremonial gifts and diplomacy. Gallery 359.
exhibitions.long_description:
Some of the bark cloths in Gallery 359 were diplomatic gifts from senior Samoan chiefs to Robert Louis Stevenson and his wife Fanny, who argued the chiefs' case while the couple lived in Samoa from 1890 to 1894. The chiefs called the author of Treasure Island "Tusitala", Teller of Tales.

Groups of women make tapa from the inner bark of the paper mulberry tree and paint it by hand. In Polynesia it is the cloth of ceremonial exchange. The Met shows 19th-century pieces from Fiji, Samoa and Futuna from its collection, adds a Niuean hiapo lent by Te Papa, and hangs a pair of large Fijian panels, masi kesa, together for the first time. Samoan chiefs gave cloth as statecraft, which sets a high bar for December's office Secret Santa.

You stay in one gallery, and it's free with Museum admission, so it fits any Met visit. Alongside the old cloths hangs a monochrome painting by the Niuean poet and painter John Puhiatau Pule, whose early work borrowed hiapo's grids.

look_for.title: The Stevenson gifts
look_for.text: Look for the boldly designed tapa that Samoan chiefs presented to Robert Louis Stevenson and Fanny as diplomatic gifts in the 1890s.

look_for.title: The masi kesa pair
look_for.text: Two large-scale Fijian bark-cloth panels, shown side by side here for the first time.

look_for.title: The hiapo from Niue
look_for.text: A Niuean bark cloth lent by Te Papa Tongarewa, New Zealand's national museum, in the grid-like design Niue is known for.

look_for.title: John Puhiatau Pule's painting
look_for.text: A contemporary monochrome by the Niuean poet and painter, whose early paintings took their cue from hiapo grids.

exhibitions.title: Rediscovering Della Robbia at The Met
exhibitions.description: Results from a collaborative exchange among curators, conservators, and digital specialists studying The Met's Della Robbia sculptures.
exhibitions.long_description:
It's one gallery of 16 works, most out of storage for the first time in decades, from three generations of the Florentine family that invented glazed terracotta around 1440. Up close you can find the seams, hidden along the outlines, where big works were fired in sections. Moulded in multiples, weatherproof and cheaper than marble, this was the flat-pack version of Renaissance sculpture, and it still gleams.

Santa Fe dealer Gerald Stiebel noted it opened without the Met's usual hoopla, and called it a presentation "one would think you could only see in Italy". It's in Gallery 521, free with Museum admission, through January 2028. Met Expert Talks on it run 13 October and 9 February 2027, 3pm.

look_for.title: The Marquand Altarpiece
look_for.text: Andrea's Assumption of the Virgin, ca. 1485: 33 newly conserved glazed sections set against a graphic rendering of the full ten-by-seven-foot altar.

look_for.title: The animated reconstruction
look_for.text: A large video built from 3D scans assembles the whole altarpiece and suggests the order the workshop put it together in.

look_for.title: Two generations, two palettes
look_for.text: Andrea's Saint Michael the Archangel hangs beside Giovanni's newly gifted Mystic Mandorla, to show the brighter range of colours Giovanni brought to the family's glazes.

look_for.title: Dovizia and St. Michael statuettes
look_for.text: The same basic figure reworked twice: Dovizia raises a hand to steady a platter of fruit, while Saint Michael swings a sword over a writhing dragon.

look_for.title: The bust of François I
look_for.text: The king of France in glazed terracotta, 1529, the only known Della Robbia portrait whose sitter was both a contemporary and firmly identified.

exhibitions.title: Our Flag Was Still There
exhibitions.description: Historic American flags tied to 9/11, including the Ground Zero Flag, paired with personal stories in Foundation Hall to mark the nation's 250th anniversary.
exhibitions.venue_address: 180 Greenwich Street, New York, NY 10007, United States
exhibitions.long_description:
The installation is in Foundation Hall and is built around four flags. You stand in the hall with the Last Column, the 36-foot steel remnant of the South Tower, and the flag that flew over it through the nine months of recovery is part of the show. So is the flag FDNY firefighters raised on the afternoon of 9/11, the one in Tom Franklin's photograph, and the Garrison flag that soldiers hung down the side of the Pentagon on September 12. Press photographs and first-person stories, such as FDNY Captain Michael Dugan's, fill in the rest.

It comes with museum admission ($24 to $36, or free on Mondays from 5:30 to 7pm, tickets released online that morning). Last entry is an hour before the 7pm close. On view through February 2028.

look_for.title: The Bin Laden Raid flag
look_for.text: Look for the handwritten "5/1/11 Geronimo 'NS'" on the flag a lead Chinook pilot carried tucked into his flight gear on the 2011 raid.

look_for.title: The Ground Zero Flag
look_for.text: The flag in Tom Franklin's photograph, shown with the 2002 USPS stamps and medals that reproduced the image, and the story of how it went from a yacht at a nearby marina to this museum.

look_for.title: The Pentagon's Garrison flag
look_for.text: A Garrison flag, the largest official U.S. flag, which soldiers of the 3rd Infantry Regiment and Arlington firefighters draped over the side of the Pentagon on September 12, 2001.

look_for.title: The Last Column flag
look_for.text: The flag raised over the 36-foot South Tower column that still stands in Foundation Hall, there until the column was removed on May 30, 2002 to mark the end of recovery.

exhibitions.title: Responding in Ink: Comic Books, Graphic Novels, and 9/11
exhibitions.description: Examines how comic book and graphic novel artists responded to 9/11, from pre-2001 fictional depictions of the World Trade Center through decades of memoirs, charitable efforts, and educational works.
exhibitions.venue_address: 180 Greenwich Street, New York, NY 10007, United States
exhibitions.long_description:
You start before 2001, with comics from the 1970s onward in which supervillains made the Twin Towers a regular target. From there about 50 covers, pages and pieces of original art follow how the industry responded: charity books published within months of the attacks, then memoirs, anniversary books and educational works. Penelope Ray, the museum's director of exhibition development, calls comics "a really important way that young readers learn about history".

It's included with museum admission ($36 for adults, free on Mondays from 5:30 to 7pm) and runs through February 2028. The museum is open Wednesday to Monday, 9am to 7pm.

look_for.title: The inked Spider-Man page
look_for.text: Uncoloured inks by John Romita Jr. and Scott Hanna from Marvel's late-2001 issue that put the city's emergency responders at the centre of the story.

look_for.title: Big Apple Diaries
look_for.text: Alyssa Bermudez's graphic memoir, built from the diary she kept as a New York middle schooler whose father worked in the World Trade Center.

exhibitions.title: A King's Carpet: Louis XIV and the Savonnerie
exhibitions.description: The first US exhibition on the Savonnerie centers The Met's three monumental Baroque carpets woven for Louis XIV's Grande Galerie at the Louvre, tracing their making and dispersal.
exhibitions.long_description:
Four complete carpets fill the Wrightsman Galleries, with fragments and a trial weave possibly made by a trainee. The Met is frank about who did the weaving: orphans and homeless children gathered from Paris streets for their sharp eyes and nimble fingers. Laid end to end, the full set would have outrun The Met's own Fifth Avenue facade.

You can also watch textile conservators repairing one carpet in a temporary studio inside the gallery. The show is in Galleries 524 to 528, included with Museum admission, and runs until March 5, 2028.

look_for.title: The Music carpet on the wall
look_for.text: Look up at Grande Galerie carpet no. 11, with Euterpe and Erato woven into nearly 30 feet of wool pile, hung vertically like a tapestry for the first time at The Met.

look_for.title: Fame and Fortitude, mid-repair
look_for.text: Carpet no. 38, the first Grande Galerie carpet to reach America and once Alva Vanderbilt's, is the one conservators are strengthening in the in-gallery studio.

look_for.title: The Landscapes carpet
look_for.text: Carpet no. 73 is one of the narrower pieces, with a landscape woven at each end; it served the French ambassador in Madrid and survived the Revolution and the Spanish Civil War.

look_for.title: Marie Antoinette's game-room rug
look_for.text: An Apollo Gallery carpet woven in 1664 to 1666, later laid in Marie Antoinette's temporary game rooms in 1785 and then owned by the Rothschilds, on loan from a private collection.

exhibitions.title: In Their Honor: 25 Years of 9/11-Inspired Service
exhibitions.description: Opened for the 25th anniversary, this exhibition explores how individuals and communities transformed grief into service inspired by 9/11, among a generation with no lived memory of the attacks.
exhibitions.venue_address: 180 Greenwich Street, New York, NY 10007, United States
exhibitions.long_description:
You look up at the wings, then turn to the screens, where a 3D model lets you pick out each artist and read where their service took them. Around it are objects from people who answered 9/11 with work: the jacket Captain Beverley Bass wore when she diverted her American Airlines flight to Gander, the bunker coat presented to Jon Stewart during his 2019 testimony to Congress, and the FDNY helmet of a son who followed his father into the department.

It's included with museum admission ($36 for adults, free on Mondays from 5:30 to 7pm) and runs through January 2030.

look_for.title: The Feathers of the Phoenix
look_for.text: Look up for the papier-mâché phoenix, 15 feet wing to wing, its feathers decorated by children who lost family on 9/11, with a 3D model on screens nearby.

look_for.title: Captain Beverley Bass's uniform jacket
look_for.text: The jacket she wore on 9/11 when she diverted her flight to Gander, Newfoundland, later worn on stage by Jenn Colella in Come From Away.

look_for.title: Ray Pfeifer's bunker coat
look_for.text: An FDNY firefighter's coat signed by 9/11 healthcare advocates and presented to Jon Stewart when he testified to Congress for responders' healthcare in 2019.

look_for.title: James Dowdell's FDNY helmet
look_for.text: The helmet of a firefighter who joined the FDNY after his father Kevin died on 9/11, and made lieutenant at Rescue 2 in 2025.

look_for.title: The Zabuli Education Center kite
look_for.text: An embroidered kite made by a student at a free school for girls in rural Afghanistan.

exhibitions.title: Rubin Museum Tibetan Buddhist Shrine Room
exhibitions.description: A six-year installation of the Rubin Museum's beloved Tibetan Buddhist Shrine Room within the Arts of Asia galleries: over 100 thangkas, sculptures, and ritual objects arranged as an elaborate household shrine, with chanted prayers, butter lamps, and incense.
exhibitions.venue_address: 200 Eastern Parkway, Brooklyn, NY 11238, United States
exhibitions.long_description:
This is the Rubin Museum's Shrine Room, seen by over a million people on 17th Street from 2013 to 2024. More than 100 objects from the 12th to 21st centuries (thangkas, gilt bronzes, drums, conch trumpets) sit on Tibetan furniture in the order of a wealthy household shrine. The current selection follows the Geluk tradition and rotates every few years. It crossed the East River with its own doors and beams, a smoother move to Brooklyn than most Manhattan renters get.

Brooklyn's Asian art curator finds it even more transporting among the museum's white walls. The collective Our Ancestors Say No wants it returned, calling the objects stolen. It's in the second-floor Arts of Asia galleries, included in untimed general admission (pay what you can at the desk), with an audio guide on Bloomberg Connects.

look_for.title: Tsongkhapa and Scenes from His Life
look_for.text: An 18th-century painted thangka of the Geluk school's founder, the tradition this arrangement follows, shown with episodes from his life.

look_for.title: The brocade hangings
look_for.text: Silk brocade textiles made by master artisans hang from the ceiling and the pillars, as they would in a Tibetan home shrine.

look_for.title: The ritual instruments
look_for.text: Look for the hand drums, conch trumpets, horns and reeds laid out with vajras, bells and offering bowls.

look_for.title: The shrine touchscreen
look_for.text: An interactive screen walks you through what a shrine's objects stand for: the Buddha's body, speech and mind.

exhibitions.title: Julie Curtiss: UNREAL
exhibitions.description: New paintings by Julie Curtiss of faceless figures in New York apartments, laundromats and bodegas, in her first presentation with Gagosian in New York, at 541 West 24th Street.
exhibitions.long_description:
In one painting, the back half of an elephant stands inside a bodega doorway, the shopfront plastered with ads for baked goods and deli sandwiches. The bodega cat has competition.

These are new paintings, Curtiss's first with Gagosian in New York, set in the city: apartments, laundromats, bodegas, a fortune teller's window. The people are cropped or turned away, so you never get a face. In Makeover, two women in fur coats, sunglasses and post-surgery compression masks stand with their backs to you. Only the animals show their faces: fish and a crab in restaurant tanks on Grand Street, and a squid fighting a whale in a bedroom, borrowed from a diorama at the American Museum of Natural History.

"Nothing feels real right now," Curtiss says, and the gallery promises sly humour to go with it. Entry is free at 541 West 24th Street, Tuesday to Saturday 10am to 6pm. The opening reception is Tuesday 10 November, 6 to 8pm, and the show runs until 19 December.

look_for.title: Bodega (2026)
look_for.text: In a flat, stark composition, an elephant's hindquarters fill a shop doorway whose outside is covered in ads for baked goods and deli sandwiches.

look_for.title: Makeover (2026)
look_for.text: Two women seen from behind in fur coats, sunglasses and postoperative compression face masks, their hair, fur and accessories painted pattern by pattern.

look_for.title: Dirty Laundry (2026)
look_for.text: Look down: a man's and a woman's formal shoes face each other on a checkerboard floor in front of a row of washing machines.

look_for.title: Squid and Whale (2026)
look_for.text: The predator fight from a Natural History Museum diorama, a scene no human has actually witnessed, moved from the ocean depths into a bedroom.

look_for.title: Grand Street (2026)
look_for.text: A restaurant kitchen at night, with tanks of fish, mussels and a crab under coloured light and roasted ducks hanging in the window.

exhibitions.title: A Long Shadow: Postwar Japan Through the Lens
exhibitions.description: Postwar Japanese photography, from Okinawa and base towns under US occupation, drawn from the Met's collection with rare photobooks and new acquisitions. Gallery 851.
exhibitions.long_description:
The Met's image for this show is Tōmatsu Shōmei's Hateruma Island, from 1971: a black-and-white sea under one huge, billowing cloud, the horizon tipped on a slant. Hateruma is in Okinawa, which the United States occupied until 1972 and which still hosts most of the American troops stationed in Japan.

Okinawa and the towns around US bases are the show's ground. Tōmatsu photographed the collision of American and Japanese culture there. Ishikawa Mao, Ishiuchi Miyako and Tokiwa Toyoko turned to what the occupation meant for women, including themselves and their friends. Yamashiro Chikako, an Okinawan artist working now, carries it into the present. Next to the prints are the photobooks and monthly magazines where photographers swapped neutral reportage for something personal.

It is the Met's first Japanese photography show since 1995, drawn from its own collection, with new acquisitions by Tōmatsu, Ishikawa and Ishiuchi. You'll find it in Gallery 851 at The Met Fifth Avenue, free with Museum admission.

exhibitions.title: Kent Monkman: Officer and Laughing Girl
exhibitions.description: New paintings by contemporary artist Kent Monkman responding to Vermeer's Officer and Laughing Girl, examining trade, colonization and Indigenous-European encounters through his alter ego Miss Chief.
exhibitions.long_description:
The painting that prompted this show hangs a short walk away. When you finish in the installation, the Frick points you to the South Hall to see Vermeer's Officer and Laughing Girl, painted around 1657, the picture Kent Monkman is answering.

Monkman's new paintings fill the Cabinet Gallery. He uses Vermeer's scene as a way into how Dutch art of the period showed the effects of global trade and colonization. His alter ego Miss Chief, who time-travels and shapeshifts, carries the story through five centuries of Indigenous and European encounters, with the cultural, technological and environmental changes that came with them.

The series travels on to the Beaverbrook Art Gallery in Fredericton, New Brunswick, with a bilingual English and Canadian French catalogue. Admission is $30 and included in general museum entry; the Frick is closed Tuesdays.
exhibitions.editors_pick: New paintings by Kent Monkman answer Vermeer's Officer and Laughing Girl. His alter ego Miss Chief enters the picture to look at trade, colonization and the encounters between Indigenous people and Europeans.

exhibitions.title: Georg Baselitz: Meine Schule
exhibitions.description: Georg Baselitz's last completed paintings and sculptures, curated by Richard Calvocoressi, at 555 West 24th Street; the gallery's first Baselitz show since his death in April.
exhibitions.long_description:
Two of the paintings show schoolchildren lined up beneath a banner reading Ein Volk, Ein Reich, Ein Führer. It hung outside the schoolhouse in Deutschbaselitz, where Baselitz's father taught and the family lived during the war. It is the artist's earliest memory, and neither painting has been shown before.

Baselitz died in April and conceived and designed this show himself, around his last completed paintings. In the rest of them, tilt your head: the couple drawn in fine black lines on gold is Baselitz and his wife, Elke, upside down, each with a burst of bright impasto he called "a misplaced Willem de Kooning". There are also two monumental bronzes, including his last sculpture, Strawinsky, a seated figure over seven feet tall whose head and limbs collapse while its trunk stays upright.

Entry is free at 555 West 24th Street, Tuesday to Saturday 10am to 6pm. The opening reception is Thursday 12 November, 6 to 8pm, and the show runs until 23 January.
exhibitions.editors_pick: The last paintings and sculptures Georg Baselitz completed, curated by Richard Calvocoressi. The first New York look at how the painter who turned his figures upside down finished his career, in a gallery that charges nothing to enter.

look_for.title: Meine Schule, die Jungs and Meine Schule, die Mädchen (2026)
look_for.text: Boys in one, girls in the other, standing before the Nazi banner hung on his father's school on days like Hitler's birthday; neither has been exhibited before.

look_for.title: Strawinsky (2026)
look_for.text: His last sculpture: a white-patinated bronze seated figure, over seven feet tall, from his puppet designs for The Soldier's Tale, its trunk upright and its head and limbs collapsing.
A second monumental bronze with the same rough, tactile surface but dark, based on Baselitz's own figure in A. R. Penck's 1964-65 group portrait of four friends.

look_for.title: The gold paintings
look_for.text: Baselitz and Elke upside down in thin, ink-like black lines on gold grounds, each interrupted by a cluster of colourful impasto he called "a misplaced Willem de Kooning".

exhibitions.title: 25th Anniversary Exhibition: Masterworks from the Neue Galerie
exhibitions.description: Opening Autumn 2026, this milestone show fills the entire museum with collection highlights, from Klimt's Adele Bloch-Bauer I to German and Austrian masterworks and Wiener Werkstaette design.
exhibitions.long_description:
The Neue Galerie has been shut since the summer for building upgrades, and its galleries open again on 12 November with a show that takes over the whole William Starr Miller House. Two exhibition floors of the 1914 Fifth Avenue mansion hold the collection's best-known pieces, with Klimt's gold-leaf Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I (1907) at the head of a list that also names Schiele, Kokoschka, Beckmann, Dix and Bauhaus artists.

It is a collection show rather than a single-theme one, so paintings hang beside design: Josef Hoffmann's 1912 gold tobacco case set with gemstones, Marianne Brandt's 1927 metal-and-wood tea infuser, a Moriz Jung greyhound printed as a postcard. Brandt's infuser is why the one in your kitchen drawer from Muji looks underdressed.

Tickets are $28, $18 for seniors and $15 for students, and the museum lists free access on 13 November. Children under 12 are not admitted. A free digital guide carries curatorial notes on key works, and Café Sabarsky has been serving again since 1 October.
exhibitions.editors_pick: For its 25th anniversary the museum hangs collection highlights on every floor, from Klimt's Adele Bloch-Bauer I to German and Austrian masterworks and Wiener Werkstätte design.

look_for.title: Klimt's Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I
look_for.text: A woman in ornate gold garments, painted in oil, gold and silver on canvas in 1907. It is the museum's signature painting.

look_for.title: Schiele's Town among Greenery (The Old City III)
look_for.text: A 1917 oil of a town seen among trees and rooftops, the Schiele on the museum's list for this show.

look_for.title: Kandinsky's Black Form
look_for.text: A 1923 abstract oil built around a dark shape, the Bauhaus-era counterweight to the Viennese gold.

look_for.title: Münter's In the Garden in Murnau
look_for.text: A 1911 garden scene in oil on board, from the Blue Rider circle's years in Murnau.

look_for.title: Moriz Jung's Greyhound
look_for.text: A 1912 chromolithograph made as a postcard: a dog on a piece of card, hung among the paintings.

exhibitions.title: Ragtime: Cakewalk in Pianoland
exhibitions.description: Early printed ragtime and cakewalk music from the John Davis Collection of Early Printed Musical African Americana, setting Ernest Hogan beside Scott Joplin.
exhibitions.long_description:
The image the Morgan chose to announce this show is a sheet-music cover: Scott Joplin's Maple Leaf Rag, printed in St. Louis in 1899, from its own shelves. Most of what surrounds it comes from one pianist's collection, the John Davis Collection of Early Printed Musical African Americana.

Seven sections in the Engelhard Gallery follow ragtime from West African rhythm and European tradition into early jazz, then out to Broadway and film. The spine is a pairing: Ernest Hogan, known as "The Father of Ragtime", wrote catchy songs for Black working-class audiences, and Joplin wrote rags meant as serious composition. The curators present both as answers to the stage stereotypes of the day.

If you would rather hear it than read it, Davis, also a guest curator, plays rags from his collection in Gilder Lehrman Hall on 18 November at 7pm ($60, $50 for members), with the show open beforehand from 5:30. Otherwise it comes with general admission, and the Morgan stays open until 8pm on Fridays.

exhibitions.title: Rothko/Gottlieb: The Surrealist Years
exhibitions.description: Paintings and works on paper by Mark Rothko and Adolph Gottlieb from 1941 to 1951, when both turned to myth and Surrealist abstraction. Curated by Arne Glimcher.
exhibitions.long_description:
In June 1943 Rothko and Gottlieb sent a joint letter to The New York Times, answering a critic who had dismissed their work. "We favor the simple expression of complex thought," they wrote, and asked for painting that was "tragic and timeless." This show covers the decade they spent trying, 1941 to 1951.

It's the sequel to last year's Realist Years, and the paintings and works on paper cluster around 1942 to 1946, when both men turned to myth and the unconscious in the shadow of the war. Gottlieb packed figures, animals and symbols into the irregular grids of his Pictographs. Rothko went organic: his Gethsemane (1945) tells the story of Christ's last hours without a single figure. If you know Rothko from the soft colour rectangles, this is what came just before them.

It's at 125 Newbury, Arne Glimcher's project space at 395 Broadway in Tribeca, on the corner of Walker Street, not Pace's Chelsea tower. Open Tuesday to Saturday, 10am to 6pm.

look_for.title: Rothko, Gethsemane (1945)
look_for.text: Christ's betrayal and final hours painted in organic, biomorphic shapes, entirely abstract, with no recognisable figure in it.

look_for.title: Gottlieb's Pictographs
look_for.text: Stylized figures, animals and symbols set in an irregular grid, closer to carved glyphs or cave paintings than to a picture; the earliest here dates from 1941.

exhibitions.title: Na Mira: NO SMOKING
exhibitions.description: Na Mira's first solo museum exhibition in New York: a newly commissioned media installation in the Kravis Studio using radio frequencies, infrared heat and holography, drawing on Korean shamanism and structural filmmaking.
exhibitions.long_description:
"I work with what is hard to see," Na Mira has said, and she means it literally: her installations are built from radio frequencies, infrared heat and holography. For her first solo museum show in New York, she filmed at sites of personal and historical significance, letting chance and desire steer the shoot.

The result is one new commission, projected across the Kravis Studio, MoMA's room for performance and moving images. Mira draws on Korean shamanic ritual and on structural film, and calls her practice "not film, not video, not performance, not text". MoMA says the aim is to break down the faithful image that propaganda and soft power depend on.

You walk into it straight from the fourth-floor collection galleries, so it fits inside an ordinary MoMA visit. It suits people who like art about how images work and fail; nobody has reviewed it yet. Seating changes with each Studio installation, and gallery stools are available on request at the Museum entrances.

exhibitions.title: The Nature of Color
exhibitions.description: An interactive exhibition on what color reveals about the natural world and ourselves, from how animals and plants use it to how it shapes mood.
exhibitions.venue_address: 200 Central Park West, New York, NY 10024, United States
exhibitions.long_description:
Stand between a red, a green and a blue light and your shadow splits into colored copies of you. That's the white room. The show first opened here in March 2020, days before the Museum closed for the pandemic, so few visitors got to see it.

It is five rooms, each a color with a theme: white for light and how your eyes read it, yellow for how color makes you feel, green for animals that hide or show off, red for what color means to people, and blue for pigments and dyes. Live animals sit among artifacts, artworks and hands-on stations. In a city that wears black from November to March, it's a rare winter afternoon when your shadow is more colorful than your coat.

It's on Floor 3 and needs a ticket on top of Museum entry: pick an entry date after November 15, then add The Nature of Color at checkout. Members get preview days on November 13 to 15.

look_for.title: The colored shadows
look_for.text: In the white room, red, green and blue lights shine on a screen, and stepping in front of them throws shadows in different colors.

look_for.title: The indigo dye table
look_for.text: In the blue room, up to six people dye and print fabric virtually, beside indigo textiles and objects from Africa, Mexico and India.

look_for.title: The red wardrobe
look_for.text: A couture gown, a football uniform, an Indian wedding lehenga, a cardinal's robe and a man's pink suit, each standing for something color signals, from power to gender.

look_for.title: The color game show

exhibitions.title: Alex Webb: Walking Blues
exhibitions.description: Magnum photographer Alex Webb's bold-colour street pictures from some forty US cities, shaped by the rhythm of blues music over more than a decade.
exhibitions.venue_address: 380 Columbus Avenue at West 78th Street, New York, NY 10024
exhibitions.long_description:
Children play in a downtown fountain in Erie, Pennsylvania, and a rainbow arcs through the spray. Alex Webb took that picture in 2010, at the start of a series he kept shooting until 2025 across some forty American cities, from El Paso and St. Louis to Philadelphia's Chinatown.

The gallery hangs a selection of prints from Webb's new Aperture book of the same name. Webb, a Magnum member since 1979, credits the "lift and pull" of blues music, and the pictures play to his long-standing strengths: bold colour, rhythm and chance encounters. You get small cities like Erie and Fort Wayne next to New Orleans and New York, seen from the sidewalk rather than the skyline.

Entry is free, Wednesday to Sunday, closed Monday and Tuesday. Webb talks with Rebecca Norris Webb at the School of Visual Arts on 8 December, and the book costs $60.

exhibitions.title: artport: A History of Internet Art
exhibitions.description: Marking the 25th anniversary of the Whitney's artport platform, this show gathers over 100 commissioned net-art works charting the evolution of internet art from 2001 to 2024.
exhibitions.long_description:
In the middle of the sixth floor, four screens stand in a rectangle. From 2009 to 2024, artists took over whitney.org for ten to thirty seconds at every New York sunrise and sunset, and 18 of those takeovers play here in sequence, with the hourly On the Hour pieces that followed them.

You walk around them through a floor laid out like floating browser windows. All 30 artport Commissions are here, some rebuilt as installations, from code works by Golan Levin and Casey Reas to AI-driven projects by Morehshin Allahyari. The Gate Pages of 2001 to 2006 were splash pages, the intro screens the early web made you sit through before Skip Intro, and here they are the art.

The show also runs online, where all 57 Gate Pages live. Admission is $30, free for visitors 25 and under and on Fridays from 5 to 10pm. The Whitney is closed Tuesdays and recommends booking ahead.
exhibitions.editors_pick: Over 100 net-art works commissioned for the Whitney's artport platform, charting internet art from 2001 to 2024 for the platform's 25th anniversary. The platform is older than most of the apps on your phone.

exhibitions.title: Imitation of Life
exhibitions.description: World premiere musical with a book by Lynn Nottage and music and lyrics by John Legend, directed by Liesl Tommy. Two mothers, one Black and one White, raise their daughters across 1920s Atlantic City and 1930s New York.
exhibitions.long_description:
Two single mothers, one Black and one White, raise their daughters together, first in what The Shed calls "the neon rush of 1920s Atlantic City", then in 1930s New York. Adrienne Warren plays Delilah, Jessica Vosk plays Bea, and the songs are John Legend's, his first score for a musical. Lynn Nottage wrote the book.

The story comes from Fannie Hurst's 1933 novel, which Universal filmed twice, in 1934 and 1959. Here Delilah's daughter Peola is played by two actors, one as a girl and one grown up. You sit in the Griffin Theater for about 2 hours 40 minutes, with one intermission.

This is the world premiere: previews start 21 November, it opens officially on 3 December and closes 3 January after six weeks. Post-show conversations follow the performances on 8, 15, 17 and 22 December. The ASL-interpreted performance is 20 December at 1pm, booked by emailing accessibility@theshed.org.

exhibitions.title: Éliane Radigue: States of Listening
exhibitions.description: Co-organized with Blank Forms, this show restages French composer Éliane Radigue's pulsating 1970s sonic installations in Dia's program space, with live synthesizer and acoustic performances.
exhibitions.long_description:
Radigue's early feedback pieces were short tape loops of slightly unequal length, left running until they slid out of sync, so the sound kept recombining into new tones. Dia is restaging two in-gallery sound installations she made at the turn of the 1970s. You walk into rooms built around low frequencies and what Dia calls their "morphing effects".

Around them runs a series of three concerts that follow where her sound went next: Propositions sonores on 5 December, the three-hour Trilogie de la mort (1985 to 1993) played by François J. Bonnet over two sessions in January, and Naldjorlak (2005) with the cellist Charles Curtis. Artforum's Theo Belci called the show "the apotheosis" of a decades-long effort to get her unreleased and overlooked work heard. Radigue died in Paris in February 2026, aged 94.

This is a show about listening rather than looking. Entry is free, Wednesday to Saturday, 12 to 6pm. The last concert, on 13 February, is at the Kitchen, not at Dia.
exhibitions.editors_pick: Dia and Blank Forms restage two of Éliane Radigue's early-1970s feedback and tape-loop installations, with concerts of her later pieces across the run. Artforum called it "the apotheosis". Admission is free.

exhibitions.title: Virgil Abloh: The Codes
exhibitions.description: A survey of Virgil Abloh's work in fashion, art, architecture and music: nearly 1,000 objects from his archive over 28,000 sq ft, including a recreation of his Paris office.
exhibitions.long_description:
Somewhere in the 28,000 square feet is Virgil Abloh's Paris office, rebuilt: the studio at Pont Neuf where he worked. Nearby, a media lab opens a selection of his raw design files to anyone who walks in, which is the point The Shed makes about him: the process was meant to be shared.

Around those two rooms are nearly 1,000 objects picked from an archive of more than 20,000, across fashion, sneakers, art, architecture, graphic design and music. You see finished pieces next to the prototypes and sketches behind them. Earlier editions ran in Miami and at the Grand Palais in Paris, and this one opens around the fifth anniversary of his death.

Tickets are timed, from $25, and the last slot of the day gets you in an hour before closing. Students and educators go free with ID and a reservation. An $85 VIP ticket drops the time slot and adds a merch item sold only with it.
exhibitions.editors_pick: About 1,000 objects from Virgil Abloh's archive across 28,000 square feet, including a recreation of his Paris office. For anyone who followed Off-White and his Louis Vuitton menswear, it lays out the working process in full.

exhibitions.title: Across Wine-Dark Seas: Art and Identity beyond Ancient Greece
exhibitions.description: Presents more than 180 exceptional works exploring art and identity beyond ancient Greece.
exhibitions.long_description:
For more than two decades, a bronze griffin's head greeted visitors at the entrance to The Met's Greek and Roman galleries. In 2025 the Met returned it to Greece, after research showed it had left the Olympia museum illegitimately in the 1930s. Now it's back on loan from Olympia, shown for the first time beside two related griffin heads. Like most people who leave New York, it only comes back to visit.

Around it are more than 180 objects from the eighth to the early fifth century BCE, when Greeks traded, settled and fought across the Mediterranean. You move region by region, from West Asia and Egypt to Italy, Spain and the Black Sea, and each section also shows how Greek artists pictured the people they met there.

Curator Seán Hemingway pitches it at people who think Greek art peaks with the Parthenon. It's in Gallery 199 at The Met Fifth Avenue and free with Museum admission. Members get preview days, December 17 to 19.
exhibitions.editors_pick: The Olympia griffin head, repatriated in 2025, is back on loan beside two related heads. Around it, more than 180 objects follow Greek art to southern Italy, Iberia and Susa, with the Ugento Zeus in the US for the first time.
